video.title: The Phone Habit That Was Ruining My Life

summary: Nick Huber and a guest (Corey) discuss breaking a phone addiction. Nick turned his phone off from 7pm to 7am, cut screen time to about 2.5 hours a day, batches texts and email into a 4:30-5pm calendar slot, and uses a notepad instead of his phone. The video contains no business idea; the takeaway is that managing attention and being hard to reach improves sleep, relationships and focus for a founder running several companies.

video.title: Gemini 4 Argon vs Claude Opus 5.5 (Which Is Better for Business?)

summary: George McConnell compares Google's Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5 across five basic-prompt tests: redesigning a mobile car-spa website, diagnosing an underperforming TikTok, generating a product video ad, building a 3D chess game, and building a music app. Gemini wins the website, TikTok analysis and video ad (the video test used Higgsfield via a Claude connector); Opus wins the chess game and guitar/drum app, though it is much slower in several tests. He ends with a tie and stresses that detailed prompts (e.g. a 13-page prompt) matter far more than the model choice. There is no real business idea; it is a tool comparison with some marketing commentary.

video.title: The BORING Way to Make $1M/Year Without a College Degree

summary: David Heacock interviews Jim Baloga, CEO and owner of three US proprietary schools (Porter and Chester Institute, YTI Career Institute, College of Court Reporting) that train skilled trades, healthcare and court reporting students. Baloga explains how he bought the court reporting school as a small platform to avoid a large US Department of Education letter of credit, then used it to acquire the larger schools he had run for about 20 years. He covers tuition, outcomes, regulatory barriers to entry, upfront cash collection, low acquisition multiples and a roll-up plan. The host's takeaway is that deep industry experience reveals opportunities, and that a trade skill is a low-risk base for entrepreneurship.

video.title: This guy beat the S&P500 for 11 years doing (almost) nothing

summary: A My First Million episode where the host recounts a retail investor (an exited founder) who made roughly 2.9 buy/sell decisions a year and claims ~21.8% annualised returns versus 13.5% for the S&P 500 over about 12 years. The hosts draw lessons on patience, circle of competence, pre-mortems (Jack Dorsey's '140 reasons Square will fail'), reversible vs irreversible decisions, and knowing 'what game you're playing'. The rest is anecdotes on Zuckerberg and Alexander Wang, Elon Musk's 'start building within 24 hours' story, motivation, and fear/panic management (the DARE method, rehearsal). There is no operating business idea; the value is in decision-making and mindset lessons.

speakers.name: Sam Parr
speakers.description: Co-host of My First Million (name not stated in transcript; inferred from the show). Tells the investor story.

speakers.name: Shaan Puri
speakers.description: Co-host of My First Million (name not stated in transcript; inferred from the show). Asks questions and shares anecdotes.

tactics.name: Deep study of a few understandable companies, then wait for price
steps: Pick only a few companies you can understand.
Study them very deeply: read annual reports and keep detailed written notes over months.
Keep watching the company and wait until the price is cheap enough.
Buy on the day the opportunity appears; otherwise do nothing.

quote.text: I study a few things that I can understand. And I study them very deeply. I keep very detailed notes and then I just wait for an opportunity.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

tactics.name: Pre-mortem before a big decision
steps: Before starting, write down every way it could fail (Dorsey wrote a list of 140 reasons Square would fail).
Use the list to design around those failure modes.
Judge decisions on the quality of the inputs or framework, not just the outcome (avoid 'resulting').

tactics.name: Sort decisions into reversible vs irreversible
steps: Classify each decision as reversible or not.
Do not agonise over reversible ones.
Spend thinking time only on the irreversible ones.

tactics.name: Rehearse the feared event in granular detail
steps: Recreate the real conditions in advance (same clothes, same meal, same environment), as George St-Pierre's coaches did.
Before a hard conversation such as a firing or negotiation, walk through the room and the motions beforehand.
Use exposure practice for phobias, such as short subway trips.

tactics.name: Define the game you are playing
steps: Ask yourself where you want to be in five years.
Name the game you are actually playing right now.
Let that game decide what you want and who you need to be, then ignore other games' metrics.

tools_mentioned.purpose: Used to analyse an exported brokerage account to count the number of decisions per year; also used to plan subway exposure routes.

tools_mentioned.purpose: Sponsored free guide of 35 principles from top investors.

warnings.warning: Mistaking movement for progress: constant activity and agonising over small decisions can crowd out the few decisions that matter.

quote.text: we oftentimes mistake movement with progress.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

warnings.warning: Don't judge decisions by outcomes alone (resulting); judge the input or framework.
Letting a failing business bleed into your daily life and routines (no trash can, air mattress) lowered productivity; fix routines first.
Beware the Dunning-Kruger overconfidence of early learners; the best admit how little they know.

lessons.lesson: Few, high-conviction decisions can beat constant activity; the reported investor averaged about 2.9 decisions a year and had three years with none.

quote.text: he only made 2.9 decisions a year.
quote.speaker: Sam Parr

lessons.lesson: Stay inside your circle of competence and be willing to say no to good opportunities you don't understand.
Write ideas down through pre-mortems and journals, and evaluate decisions on process rather than outcome.
Triage decisions by reversibility; don't agonise over reversible ones.
Investing rewards avoiding losses, while entrepreneurship rewards a few huge wins, so many mistakes are acceptable if the big bets pay off.
Strong leaders seek input widely from smart people, including less accomplished ones, and use the answers to gauge who gives high-signal advice.
Motion beats waiting for direction: start building quickly after a setback, since direction becomes clearer once you are in motion.

quote.text: It's about motion, not direction. And once you're in motion, it's a lot easier to figure out direction.
quote.speaker: Shaan Puri

lessons.lesson: When a business is struggling, stack small life wins (routine, exercise, tidy space) rather than waiting for outcomes to change.
Feared events are often worse in anticipation; rehearsal, acceptance and leaning into the feeling reduce fear.
Know the game you are playing; different games demand different traits and most people never define theirs.

evidence_quality.rationale: No business idea. video.title: He Makes $16K/Month Renting Out a Space He Doesn’t Own

summary: Justin Hall (The Hall ATL) rented a 3,000 sq ft former church unit in a Stone Mountain, Georgia strip mall and converted it into an event venue for birthdays, baby showers, repasses, anniversaries, weddings and fashion shows, while keeping his 9-5 job. He claims about $16K/month average revenue (about 50% net margin) with only his wife helping. Key tactics: organic build-in-public Instagram, cheap Facebook/Instagram ad specials, direct mail aimed at milestone birthdays, a QR-code photo wall that generates repeat leads, and recurring Sunday church rentals that cover rent. Main takeaways: parking, zoning/licensing and lease terms matter more than the building, and local competitors' weak marketing and booking systems are the opening. All figures are self-reported and unverified.

lessons.lesson: Restaurant economics: with 35%+ food cost, labour, insurance and utilities, even a landmark with about $3.9M in eight months nets about 18% before tax.

Do not add menu items just to fill slow seasons; add-ons and combos raise revenue with less complexity.
Commodity input costs can triple in a few years, so price flexibility and supplier relationships matter.

Weather and external shocks can swing sales by 25-30%, so reserves matter.

video.title: The Day I Almost Quit Entrepreneurship

summary: Nick Huber (Sweaty Startup) is interviewed about the two times he nearly quit entrepreneurship. The first was in Boston at Storage Squad, a student pick-up and delivery storage business, where a run of truck accidents and a customer-service overload caused a breakdown. The second was his first ground-up self-storage development in New York, which ran about 44% over its $1.7M budget and seven months late. He also describes his path from being broke after investing $500K into storage to about $30K/month by 2020, and says entrepreneurship is not right for 95% of people.

video.title: Nobody Knows You Own These BORING Businesses, Level by Level

summary: A dramatised, level-by-level narrative about acquiring retiring owners' small service businesses (pest control route, pest company, HVAC company, plumbing company) while keeping the founder's name and staff, and staying in the background. It uses market-range figures (BizBuySell medians, multiples, SBA 7(a) 10% down with seller standby notes) to show how a holding company could reach roughly $740k a year of owner earnings in 11 years. Key takeaway: buy what someone is ready to leave, keep the name and people, retain key technicians, and make sure the business doesn't live in the owner's head. It is an illustrative, US-centric story, not a first-hand operator account.

video.title: 6 signs natural moneymakers have. Do you?

summary: A My First Million episode where the host (Sean Puri) coins the term 'natural money maker' and lists its attributes: unemotional about money, high hit rate, instinctive 'nose' for deals, maximizer mindset, comfort with complexity. Examples include a trader friend who made a ~$100M ETF arbitrage and built a top restaurant, Syed Balkhi, Carl Icahn, Jay Gould and Charlie Munger. The hosts then sketch other entrepreneur archetypes (missionary, extreme balancer, tank, trickster, fierce nerd, deep student, sniffer) and argue for working with your nature. It is mostly a personality and mindset discussion; the business examples are anecdotal and second-hand.

video.title: She Makes $2K Every Saturday From Her Parents' Front Porch

summary: Chris Koerner visits Angela, a 20-year-old in Frisco, Texas, who runs 'Little Bit Bakery', a home micro bakery selling from a self-built cart on her parents' front porch every Saturday. She claims about $2,000-2,100 in sales per Saturday with roughly $500 in ingredient and packaging costs, selling out by about 9am, after a single local TikTok video took off. The video covers pricing, pre-orders via Hotplate, Texas cottage food law, a step-by-step start plan, and why hyper-local proximity businesses work. Key takeaway: a low-overhead, locally marketed home food business with weekly pre-orders can gross well, but it is very labour-intensive and physical.

Payments via Venmo/Zelle/Hotplate would be swapped for Stripe/SumUp/bank transfer, and Nextdoor exists in the UK. Honour-system stand and prices need adjusting.

video.title: I built this app for my dad. Now it makes $18K/month

summary: Starter Story host Gus interviews Kurosh, a London-based product manager who built Boise (transcribed as 'Voice C'), a cross-platform dictation app using OpenAI's Whisper API, as a side project. It reportedly makes 16-20K USD per month including lifetime deals, with 11K MRR. He competes with well-funded tools like Whisper Flow by targeting seniors and people with disabilities, who see dictation as a painkiller rather than a vitamin. Growth comes mainly from SEO (about 200 blog posts, 30 landing pages, localisation), plus the Chrome Web Store, Reddit and a new YouTube series. Key takeaways: talk to users to discover your real customer, a crowded market can be won by serving a neglected niche, and take action in volume rather than strategising.

video.title: Why I Switched to Base44 in 2026 (Full Honest Review)

summary: Mikey No Code explains why he moved from Lovable to the AI app builder Base44 in 2026. He says Lovable was good for prototypes but became costly and fragile once projects needed databases, authentication and backend logic, because small changes caused regressions that burned credits. He demos a tech-summit app (Event Pulse) with a database, bookmarking, authentication, a private portal and a redesign. He says Base44 kept everything working and built it in under 15 minutes. The video is largely a product review and also promotes his own Base44 master class, so the claims are one-sided and promotional.

Each is framed around the 'short need rent' idea: customers need an item briefly, so one owner rents it repeatedly. Figures come from third-party price trackers, trade sources and illustrative arithmetic, plus a possibly fictional narrator persona ('Harry') whose dumpster story and earnings are presented as personal anecdote. video.title: EP 565 Make Money Online With a Micro App | Validate Before Building

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur episode 565 argues that AI makes building apps fast but does not create demand, so aspiring micro-app founders should validate before building. It settles the 'validate vs copy an existing app' debate by saying existing apps prove a market but not that anyone will buy from you. It lays out a five-step test: micro-problem filter, proof checklist, switch conversation, smallest paid promise (pre-sale, do-it-by-hand, or specific waitlist), and a pre-set build/don't-build pass mark. The only worked example is a hypothetical $5/month game-day confirmation tool for youth cheer coaches.

summary: A short promo clip from Dark Horse Entrepreneur (episode 564) arguing that building a digital product quickly with AI is not evidence of demand. The host sets out three levels of evidence (existing spend, pain in buyers' own words, and commitment such as sign-ups, booked calls or pre-orders), says friends' opinions are worth nothing, and advises writing a go/no-go criterion before testing. The action is to write one sentence stating the buyer, price and result, plus the evidence that would prove you wrong. It is a validation framework, not a specific business, and ends by pointing to the full episode and a freebie.

tactics.name: Three-level evidence ladder for demand validation
steps: Level one: check for existing spend, meaning people already paying for something close to your idea; competition shows the market exists.
Level two: collect pain in buyers' own words from forums, reviews and comments, without prompting them.
Read the three-star reviews of competing products to see what buyers wanted but did not get.
Level three: get commitment, such as a specific sign-up, a booked call, or a pre-order (the gold standard).
Treat opinions, such as a friend saying they would buy, as level zero that does not count.

quote.text: Real evidence comes in three levels. Level one, there's existing spend.
quote.speaker: Host

tactics.name: Pre-commit a go/no-go criterion
steps: Before testing anything, write your go / fix / park / kill criteria on a sticky note.
Decide what counts as a yes before you see results so you do not grade on a curve afterwards.
Treat a 'kill' result as a win because you learn it in a weekend rather than after six months.

quote.text: Decide what counts as a yes before you see results because if you decide after you see results, your brain is going to grade on a curve every single time.
quote.speaker: Host

video.title: The Most Profitable Business You Can Run From a Phone

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Eli, a former Connecticut real estate agent and truck dispatcher who built a trailer-subleasing business. He leased 53ft semi-trailers from a big lessor for about $350/month, rented them to truckers for about $180/week, and found customers through Facebook Marketplace and then Facebook ads. He claims about 300 trailers, $250k/month in billings and $40-50k/month net profit with two virtual employees, run from his phone. Key takeaways: net-30 supplier terms plus upfront deposits and weekly billing give immediate positive cash flow; GPS tracking and insurance structure matter; paid ads were the scaling lever.

summary: A narrated, fictionalised 'level by level' story of building a quiet portfolio of boring cash-flowing businesses over about 12 years: a holding-company structure, a small snack vending route, laundromats bought with SBA 7(a) loans, then car washes. Each level is illustrated with US market-range numbers and an 'opponent' (rival vendor, seller's cash claims, landlord, new competitor, key-staff departure, private equity). Key takeaways are to verify revenue with utility bills, make the lease outlast the loan, and use paperwork and checklists rather than fighting competitors. video.title: Don't Build Anything Until You Do This | Digital Product Validation

summary: Dark Horse Entrepreneur host explains a weekend plan to validate a small digital product (ebook, template pack, prompt library, mini course) before building it. Evidence must cost the buyer something: existing spend, specific pain in their own words, or commitment (email, call, pre-order, payment). The plan sets go/fix/kill thresholds on Friday, researches buyers on Saturday, then writes a one-paragraph offer, builds a mock-up and landing page, and asks for a real commitment on Sunday. Key takeaway: opinions are worthless, pre-sales are the strongest evidence, and a killed idea is a cheap win.

video.title: How to Use ChatGPT Dots to Build Apps in Minutes (AI + No Code)

summary: Mikey No Code demonstrates a workflow where an AI assistant called 'Dots' (ChatGPT Dots, as titled) researches app ideas and writes three phased build prompts, which are then pasted into the no-code builder Base 44 to build a 'branded carousel maker' web app. The app is built in three phases: manual editor, brand kit/presets/projects, and PDF/PNG export plus JSON backup. The key takeaway is that better upfront decisions (narrow idea, phased prompts with clear limits) matter more than the build speed. The video is also a promotion for the presenter's paid Base 44 master class (offered free via link). No revenue or market validation data is given.

video.title: Every successful startup starts with this one advantage

summary: Jeff Harmon (Harmon Brothers ad agency, co-founder of Angel Studios) tells My First Million hosts how he built marketing campaigns for Orbrush, Poopourri, Squatty Potty and Purple Mattress, and how Angel Studios funds and markets films through a member 'guild'. The central framework is 'find your glitch': spot a channel or market gap others ignore, such as early YouTube ads costing under a penny a view, and use it as a beachhead. He also covers a comedian-led ad creation retreat, celebrity face-warming for algorithms, vibe-coding with agents overnight, and mindset lessons about letting go of disputes. Most figures are self-reported and the transcript is auto-generated with some errors.

video.title: I Let Strangers Pitch Me Their Business Live

summary: The Koerner Office hosts a live pitch event in Utah. Ten strangers get 2 minutes to pitch and 10 minutes of critique from Chris Koerner, Nick and Brandon. The pitches range from an operating VA-funded massage business doing about $68k/month and a $1.5M ARR home-service marketing agency to pre-revenue ideas such as a seed cup, an NFC keychain, a containment diaper, a choose-your-path kids' letter subscription, an AI relationship app and mail-in cast iron cleaning. The hosts invested in or offered to help several, and the audience voted Go Seeds first, Pick a Path Letters second and Utah Veterans Massage third. The main takeaways are that distribution (especially paid ads and short-form video) is the recurring bottleneck, and that investors want proof of a repeatable process before funding. All numbers are unverified pitch claims.

video.title: 6 BORING Things You Buy Once and Rent Out Every Weekend (Back in Your Driveway by Monday)

summary: A listicle-style video pitching six asset-rental side businesses that live in a driveway and run on a Friday handover and Monday return: bounce house, party tents/tables/chairs, tool kits, portable hot tub, utility trailer and camper. For each it gives rental rates, purchase costs, payback periods, who books, handover and reset routines, and a 'moat' (insurance, paperwork, deposits). It includes a failure story about skipping deposit and photos, a three-filter selection framework and a composite 'Harry' narrative. Figures are mostly generic, second-hand or illustrative, and the story is a narrated composite, so treat numbers as claims. Key takeaway: buy a cheap used asset, require insurance, deposit and photos, and stagger seasonal assets.

video.title: It Took Me 20 Years to Master Business. You Get It In 25 Minutes

summary: David Heacock, founder of Filterbuy (US air filter manufacturer, claimed ~150,000 filters/day and ~$25M/month revenue), shares five stages of building a boring business: commit long enough to learn, fund the constraint, build systems that preserve judgment, don't diversify before the core is ready, and build resilience and legacy. He recounts leaving Goldman, buying a declining $300k/yr business with debt, taking $50k salary for 7.5 years, and losing millions in 2021 by launching a freight company and buying an HVAC business while the core was doubling. Key takeaway: do the work yourself first, turn judgment into systems, and put capital into the core constraint rather than diversifying early.

video.title: 3 BORING Operator Rules Costco, Walton, and Gates Used to Win

summary: A compilation video of three operator-playbook essays using Costco's Jim Sinegal, Sam Walton, Bill Gates, Charlie Munger and others as case studies. Part one covers four hiring/retention rules and a 'rehire score' exercise; part two argues small businesses beat bigger rivals by copying proven ideas and shipping them better (the 'steal and ship loop'); part three sets out three trust rules (one unbreakable promise, refuse excess margin, spend on existing customers) illustrated with a fictional auto-repair owner. There is no real business idea or first-hand operator data; it is generic small-business advice built on a fictional character 'Harry' and secondhand statistics.

video.title: The Wealthiest People I Know All Did This

summary: Nick Huber (Sweaty Startup) answers two questions in a short excerpt: how to find and manage business partners, and whether to focus on one business or branch out. He says partners are hard to find and fail for moral reasons or because the value equation is off, and that splitting equity too many ways in small businesses leaves nobody making money. He notes that only 3 of his 11 companies matter financially (power law), four are unprofitable, and that 8 of 10 wealthy people he knows focused on one business. He pivoted out of a brutal student moving and storage business into self-storage. Key takeaway: focus on a good business, pick partners carefully, and stay open to better opportunities as momentum builds.

video.title: He Makes $27K/Month Sending Text Messages

summary: Aaron Fuks of Hyros (Denver) explains how he built a B2B referral-pipeline business for home service trades (siding, painting, electrical, landscaping). He cold calls and mass-texts businesses in adjacent trades, gets a real bid or project first, then uses it as proof to sell partner introductions to a client. Pricing moved from $150 per appointment to $6,000 for 10 intros plus a $250-500/month nurturing fee, with claimed revenue around $27K last month. Key takeaway: bring value first (a real bid), sell relationships rather than leads, and run it on GoHighLevel with minimal cost.

video.title: Forget Storage Units. He Rents Out Empty Dirt Instead?!

summary: UpFlip host walks through Chris Conrad's 'Long Yards' business, which rents fenced, gated dirt lots (storage yards) to contractors and other tenants on month-to-month terms. Chris explains how he found tenants early on (approaching vehicles, flyers at Home Depot, online marketplaces), how land is evaluated (net rentable square footage, NOI, cap rate) and how deals can be done via purchase, lease or profit share with landowners using investor money. He claims one Canadian flagship nets $25k/month at a 62% margin and that he works about five hours a week with on-the-ground staff. The key takeaway is that the model is simple operationally but is really a land and real estate business that needs capital, partners and underwriting skill.

speakers.description: Founder of Long Yards, former carpenter and general contractor from Canada, now expanding into the US

speakers.name: UpFlip host

ideas.name: Contractor storage yards (Long Yards)
ideas.one_liner: Rent fenced, gated plots of dirt by the month to contractors and other businesses that need outdoor storage for vehicles, trailers and equipment.
ideas.business_model: Month-to-month rent per yard, sticky long-term tenants, with extra income from boxes and offices.
ideas.customer: Contractors, civil workers, tow truck and bus operators, car businesses, service businesses, and some homeowners with RVs or toys.
ideas.problem: Contractors and others cannot find secure, affordable outdoor storage for big equipment, trailers and fleets; supply is constrained.
ideas.offer: Gated, fenced yards of 1,000 to 5,000+ sq ft with power outlets, cameras, automatic gate lockout for non-payment, month-to-month flexibility.

pricing.model: Monthly rent per yard, varying by size and market
pricing.notes: Price is set by starting high and lowering until the lead-to-visit-to-close conversion rate hits target; tenants range from $25/month early on to $5-6k/month.

acquisition_channels.details: Early on Chris ran up to vehicles at red lights, approached tow truck drivers, and walked the Home Depot car park asking drivers with trucks if they need a storage yard; left flyers in door handles.

quote.text: I would literally run up to vehicles at a red light and be like, Hey, you need a storage yard.
quote.speaker: Chris Conrad

acquisition_channels.details: Posted on online marketplaces (Facebook Marketplace, Kijiji-style classifieds) to get the first few tenants.
Now spends roughly $500 to $1,000 a month; says Google, Facebook and listing sites perform best for ROI. Previously spent tens of thousands per month at some locations with poor results.
Classified and listing sites (transcript garbles names, e.g. 'classy and loop') produce leads.
Larger contractors now reach out directly; tenants are sticky and expand within the site.

ideas.delivery: Chris builds fenced yards on leased or owned land, with gates, power outlets and cameras. On-site staff (Eddie) keep sites clean and check security; an ops/sales assistant and a phone person handle enquiries and site visits. Tenants almost always visit before renting and are closed on site after qualifying questions (problem, solution, size, timing).
unit_economics_claims: Flagship Canada site nets $25k/month at 62% margin
US site: land about $1M, total about $3.5M, expected value $6.5M when leased up
Build-out payback on boxes about 1.5 to 2 years
Whiteboard example: 92,000 net rentable sq ft x $0.25 = about $23k/month, about $20k at 90% occupancy, about $16k NOI after $4k expenses
ideas.startup_cost: Very high for buy and build: about $3.5M for the US site and about $500k for another location. Lease route example about $350k total project with a 10% (about $35k) down payment. Chris says it can be done with investor or partner money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Depends on build and permits; early yards were pre-sold to afford front gates, and the Canadian winter delayed things. Existing warehouse could be rented temporarily while permits take 3 months to 3 years.

acquisition.how: Inbound paid search, listings and SEO can be agent-run, but tenants insist on visiting in person and a human closes on site.

onboarding.how: Site tours, qualifying questions and on-site closing are human-led; only contracts and payment setup can be automated.

delivery.how: Requires physical land, fencing, build-out, permits, site cleanup and security by people on the ground.

billing.how: Recurring rent and automatic gate lockout for non-payment can be automated.

support.how: Phone enquiries (5 to 8 a day per site) and site issues are mostly handled by staff; some triage could be AI-assisted.

uk_applicability.notes: Concept (outdoor storage for vans, plant, trailers) exists, but SBA financing, US land and zoning economics are not transferable. UK needs planning permission/change of use for storage land, business rates, and land is scarce and costly. Landowner profit-share or lease approach could work with changes but needs large capital.

risks: Huge capital needs and real estate debt exposure
Chris himself filed a consumer proposal after earlier losses
Zoning, permits and wetlands/setbacks limit usable land
Land scarcity makes deals hard to find
Dependent on a single local market's demand and rates
Environmental issues such as fluids leaking onto land

tactics.name: Underwrite land with net rentable sq ft
steps: Measure usable acres and convert to sq ft (3 acres = 130,680 sq ft)

Deduct expenses (about $4k/month in example) to get NOI
Multiply NOI by 12 and divide by cap rate (8%) to find what the dirt is worth and what you can offer

video.title: I built this website in 8 hours with Claude. Now it makes $40K/month

summary: Starter Story host Gus interviews Frank Michael Smith, a non-technical sports creator who built Geogames (Geosports, Geohistory and others), a daily five-question map-tap trivia web game, in about eight hours with Claude. He claims about $40K/month (roughly $30-35K programmatic ads plus about 1,800 Pro subs via Stripe) and 700K monthly active users. Growth came from word-of-mouth sharing (53% share rate), playability inside X, and a 'host' programme where sports personalities write the daily questions and retweet. Key takeaways: build for web, build in shareability, start now, and stay in the game long-term.

video.title: People are doing $100M+ in sales on this app (ft. Whatnot founder)

summary: Grant LaFontaine, founder of Whatnot (live-shopping marketplace, claimed ~$20B valuation), tells the story of starting it with Logan Head after abandoning a full-service Craigslist idea because delivery economics failed. They chose Funko Pops from eBay sales data, solved the marketplace chicken-and-egg problem by being the first seller, and grew buyers through YouTube influencers and a viral share-to-enter giveaway. Live selling launched in July 2020 and drove growth to roughly $1B in sales within about two years. The key takeaways are to start in a tiny niche, seed one side of a marketplace yourself, be customer-driven rather than vision-driven, and use unscalable growth hacks early. The host also lists ecosystem opportunities around Whatnot: wholesale supply marketplaces, multi-channel networks and tools.

video.title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

summary: My First Million hosts Sean Puri and Shaan interview Joe Hudson, founder of Art of Accomplishment, an executive coach whose clients include Sam Altman and leaders from OpenAI and other AI labs. The conversation covers limiting beliefs, the self-reliance pattern, feeling avoided emotions, visualising worst cases, handling conflict, negative self-talk and running weekly self-experiments. Hudson also describes his path from meditation to VC to coaching. The key business takeaway is that executive coaching and group programmes for founders and exec teams is the one business discussed, and the video is mainly personal-development advice rather than a replicable business playbook.

summary: A short promotional teaser warning that people searching how to make money with ChatGPT are being targeted by malware, fake apps and fake browser extensions that steal ChatGPT logins. summary: Codie Sanchez explains her '6M' framework for selling anything online, drawn from the launch of her second book (Owner Beyond ... ) via a free virtual event with a $1M giveaway. The Ms are: magnet (reciprocity/exclusivity/self-referencing ads), message (customer is the hero, benefit before feature), micro-commitment (get a small first yes, then upsell), make the ask (clear, longer CTAs with six rules), money (margin and owning customer data), and map (90/60/30/10 launch content calendar). Key takeaway: lead with a valuable free give, sell the customer's ideal state, step up asks gradually, and protect margin and customer ownership. Mostly marketing/launch advice rather than a specific business idea, and the claims are self-reported and promotional.

video.title: This AI Finds the Idea, Customers, and Does the Work

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alex from Hyper Agent (built by Airtable), a platform for persistent, named AI agents that browse the web, spin up sub-agents and run on schedules ('live mode'). Demos include an agent that finds local businesses with great reviews but no or poor websites and builds them new sites, an always-on 'Signal' outbound sales agent that builds personalised landing pages per prospect, a pond-dredging lead database proof of concept, and a Facebook Marketplace scout. Chris then uses Hyper Agent to research boring $500k businesses, builds a laundromat opportunity map and saves it as a daily 'Deal Scout' agent. Key takeaway: treat agents as 24/7 employees with narrow permissions, and use them for lead generation, personalised outreach and agency delivery; the content is largely a product demo with promotional bias.

video.title: This Ridiculously Simple Business Makes Him $4M/Year (Can’t Fail)

summary: David Heacock interviews Ian Dolberg, founder of Dolcore, a New York City (Staten Island) security guard agency started in 2018 after military service and years working for large guard firms. Revenue went from $90k in year one to about $670k, then $1.3M, then nearly $4M in 2024, dipping to $3.3M last year as client funding was cut. Ian describes cold-calling sales, shotgun hiring, regulatory barriers, thin margins (~7%) and price-driven RFP losses. He also launched a marketing agency (Black Op Digital) for other guard companies. The host pushes him on value proposition, retention and systems. Key takeaway: a people-heavy, regulated, low-margin service that grew via founder-led outbound sales and niche compliance moats, but it is not agent-automatable.

ideas.name: Dolcore security guard agency (NYC)
ideas.one_liner: Licensed security guard staffing for NYC businesses, nonprofits, schools, cannabis, residential and events.
ideas.business_model: Hourly bill rate to clients for supplied guards; margin is the markup over guard wages, insurance, uniforms and equipment.
ideas.customer: NYC businesses and institutions needing licensed guards: cannabis dispensaries, supportive housing and shelters, private schools, retail, banks, co-ops/HOAs, residential buildings, event organisers, nonprofits.
ideas.problem: Businesses need legally licensed guards reliably present; a single in-house guard calling out leaves them unprotected or unable to open, and in-house forces carry insurance and licensing burdens.
ideas.offer: Licensed, military-led guards from a pool of about 200, with callout cover, 24/7 central monitoring of guards, supervisors, SOPs, training and paperwork for prevailing-wage contracts; plus bespoke tech such as a vibe-coded gate access control system.

pricing.model: Hourly bill rate over guard wage; tiered guard experience levels; competitive bidding via RFPs

price_points.label: 24-hour guard service for first residential client
Access control system the incumbent charged a gated community

pricing.notes: Race to the bottom on bid rates; minimum wage rises push prices up and clients shop around.

acquisition_channels.details: Founder cold-called facilities managers, property managers and security directors; sent a letter and packet/trifold beforehand announcing a call time, then called; weekly batches of 10 LinkedIn-sourced contacts. Now a hired salesperson trained in his method (outbound calls and emails).
Connected with property managers on LinkedIn, pulled emails into an Excel sheet and followed up.
Paid $50 to join the Metropolitan Cemetery Association to reach cemetery directors; Staten Island Chamber of Commerce, golf committee and event sponsorships.
In-house SEO team plus Google Ads; about $135k a year on marketing; aims to respond to quote requests within 15 minutes.
Friend introductions (bank client via Statland Security owner, Snug Harbor event); guards alert him when a site gets a new security director.
Invited to many RFPs; bid about $100M in RFPs this year and won none because of price; DCAS-certified school list gives grant-funded school work.
Event videos and a guard music video on website, YouTube and social, linked in proposals instead of stock photos.

ideas.delivery: Humans physically staff posts. Dispatch runs 24 hours, central monitoring watches guards, supervisors (mostly veterans) do random night inspections. Hiring via personal network, sponsored Indeed posts and social media, with interviews at coffee shops initially.
unit_economics_claims: About 7% margin, which he says could be adjusted up to about 19%
$8k per week of revenue is roughly $400k a year, giving about $28k profit at 7%
2024 revenue just under $4M, 2025 $3.3M, projected a little over $4M this year
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (security agency licence obtained; first year funded by cold calling while employed as an investigator)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About one month after quitting, three cemetery contracts began (April 2018 start).

acquisition.how: Inbound SEO and ads can be automated, but his proven method is human phone outreach to decision makers and RFPs; cold email to limited companies is legal in the UK but calls need TPS screening.

onboarding.how: Needs licensed guards recruited, vetted, trained and placed at physical sites; contracts and site walkthroughs are mostly human.

delivery.how: Physical guarding by licensed humans; agents could only help with scheduling, monitoring and reporting.

billing.how: Hourly invoicing and payroll (including prevailing-wage paperwork) can be largely software-driven.

support.how: Callouts, guard no-shows and client complaints need a human dispatcher in real time.

uk_applicability.notes: UK equivalent exists, with Security Industry Authority licensing for guards and approved contractor scheme, Working Time/minimum wage rules and thin margins; NYC-specific laws (Security Guard Act, FO4 fire guard, DCAS, prevailing wage) do not apply. The model works with changes but is labour-heavy.

risks: Margins around 7% and commodity price competition from PE-backed consolidators
Client funding cuts and new security directors causing contract loss
High insurance costs and liability, for example nightclub premiums after the Astroworld incident
Guard callouts and the difficulty of staffing sites
Dependence on the founder for sales
Event work is lumpy and was an existential risk when staffing needs tripled

video.title: Forget Snack Machines. This One Refills Itself

summary: Chris Koerner interviews CJ, a Fort Worth operator of four outdoor ice and water vending machines (Everest, Cooler Ice, Twice the Ice, and a large Ice House America-style unit) with no employees beyond one part-time maintenance tech. CJ explains how he got in via his pool-service business's ice spend, why buying distressed existing machines and locations beats building from scratch, how revenue-share vs flat-rent leases work, and the claimed ~90% gross margins. He also covers sale multiples of 2-3x annual profit, avoiding financing, and low-cost entry from $500-$1,000 for a used small machine. Key takeaway: location and buying out stressed single-machine owners are the main levers, but the business needs physical servicing.

video.title: I Just Sold a Niche Software Tool for $2.7 Million…Here’s How

summary: Spencer Haws of Niche Pursuits tells how he built and sold Link Whisper, a WordPress internal-linking plugin, for $2.7 million in January 2025. He covers three ways to find software ideas (scratch your own itch, find a gap in big players' features, interview customers), seven marketing strategies, and the broker-led sale process, which was slowed by an SBA loan, a bank switch and a slow buyer's attorney. Key takeaway: a niche plugin with an existing audience, a strong product and affiliate/marketplace distribution reached about $90k/month and an exit via Quiet Light.

video.title: Unfortunately, Sales Really Is This Simple (4 Steps)

summary: Codie Sanchez explains a four-part sales framework: fix mindset (don't sell from your own wallet, sell from confidence not need), fix the message (current state, future state, bridge, with the buyer stating the gap and numbers), fix the proof (named, faced, specific testimonials plus anti-sales), and fix the avatar (find people already in pain, sell oxygen not dessert). She promotes her Boardroom community, an upcoming book and a HubSpot growth kit. Key takeaway: ask questions so the buyer sells themselves, price against the cost of the problem, and target buyers already feeling the pain.

tactics.name: Ask-reframe loop to handle 'too expensive'
steps: When the buyer says it's too expensive, ask what it costs them each month to not solve the problem
Get them to state a number and total it over the delay period
Reframe their own words back and compare to your price
Ask the next question and repeat until they close themselves; don't defend or attack

quote.text: you're going to redo their words into your next words and then ask the question again.
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Current state / future state / bridge discovery
steps: Ask questions to get the prospect to reveal the current pain: who is involved, where time and money are lost, how much
Get them to say a number; write it down and show it to them
Ask about the future state without pitching
Only then present your product as the bridge, restating their numbers

quote.text: the bridge starts to write itself because you're just restating their own numbers back to them
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

steps: Use testimonials with name, photo and screenshot
Add before/after photos, payment links showing amounts, or video
Turn testimonials into stories with numbers

steps: State openly who should not buy
Target people already in pain with a budget
Score prospects as financially ready, reliable, right fit, energising

quote.text: You don't sell anyone anything. You find the people already predisposed to what the thing that you are selling.

video.title: Make Money With This New AI Agent That Works 24/7

summary: Chris Koerner tries the agentic AI tool he calls 'Grok Bot' for the first time and uses it to build a 'Morning Lock' product: a Mac menu bar app plus Chrome extension that locks Gmail and the Mail app outside set hours (e.g. 5-10am), with an accountability password held by a spouse. He had Claude write the prompt, then Grok Bot built, tested and fixed the app via Replit, GitHub and Stripe in about 31 minutes of recording. He says he plans to sell it as a SaaS in a part two, but no sales or revenue are shown. The takeaway is that agentic AI can produce a working, personally useful software product from one detailed prompt; whether it sells is untested.

video.title: Build Real Revenue in Just 15 Minutes a Day (No Ads, No Audience)

summary: Nick Loper (Side Hustle Show host) interviews Kyle, founder of a partnership-matching platform (Spark), about a four-stage partnership framework: Discover, Verify, Launch, Amplify (DVLA). The idea is to borrow existing audiences and trust via partners rather than build an audience first. Examples are given for pressure washing (realtor referral at 20%), subscription ecommerce (box-insert swaps), and a content membership (mom-influencer affiliates), with a four-bullet outreach template and a 15-minute-a-day routine. Takeaway: lead with value, run a small time-boxed minimum viable partnership, measure, then scale. The guest sells a partnership platform, so the advice is partly promotional.

summary: Codie Sanchez shares career and business lessons from her first 40 years, drawn from finance (Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse) and building her own companies. Themes include risk and family, being around winners in person, self-advocacy, negotiating on outcomes, promoting your work, keeping emotions out of work, moving fast, hiring A players and firing quickly, and rejecting work-life balance in the building phase. There is no specific business idea; the video promotes her book 'Owner Beyond' and a live launch event with a $1M giveaway.

summary: David Heacock, founder of air filter company Filterby, explains why he wants to spend his profits on a large farm and argues that agriculture's real wealth lies in land, water rights, processing, branding and distribution rather than the raw commodity. He gives examples (almond dynasties, bee pollination rental, cattle land owners, pecan orchards) and says he would pick land near Charlottesville, Virginia, of about 1,000 acres, spend the first years improving soil, water and infrastructure, then layer on diversified livestock, orchards and a direct-to-consumer brand. The key takeaway is a long-horizon, ownership-minded, asset-compounding mindset; it is a motivational pitch, not an operational playbook.

summary: UpFlip host Paul visits Emily and Jeff of Lancaster Cupcake in Pennsylvania, a 15-year-old business that grew from home baking after a Ponzi-scheme loss and a $1,400 start to roughly $3.5M revenue. The video covers production (a $20k depositor, a $60k walk-in oven, up to 6,000 cupcakes a day), cupcake trucks, three retail sites, a full P&L showing about 40% claimed margin, and the Profit First cash-flow method. Marketing relies mainly on a 50,000-person email list and a loyalty program. A flavour-creation challenge fails comically. Key takeaway: a physical, labour-heavy product business with strong repeat-customer email marketing and disciplined cost control.

video.title: I Found the Perfect First Business for Introverts

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Schuetter, a 24-26 year old introverted Cincinnati ex-hospital project manager ($52k/yr) who now earns roughly $10-15k/month as an AI implementation consultant and educator. He started by having ~100-150 free, non-salesy video calls with people in his personal network and business groups, converting about 12 into paying clients (~$25k lifetime from the first 12). His offers are private AI coaching ($5-10k/month), month-long cohort groups ($1,000 per seat), and one-off implementation builds ($1k-$20k), organised around his DASA framework (Diagnose, Articulate, Systemize, AI). Key takeaway: relationship-led, value-first outreach plus education and free content can win clients without sales experience, though the model is human-led and network-dependent.

video.title: Watch Me Clone a $200K/Month Business in 5 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner walks through GoHighLevel's public SaaSpreneur awards page, which lists white-label resellers by customer tier (gold 100+, platinum 500+, diamond 1,000+). He estimates revenue by multiplying public pricing by tier customer counts, then reverse-engineers businesses selling to local service niches: event rentals (Event Hawk), med spas, gyms (PushPress) and dental (Dental Implant Machine). His toolkit is the pricing page, Wayback Machine, Meta Ads Library, BuiltWith and LinkedIn. He ends with a live demo of a missed-call-text-back setup for roofers in GoHighLevel. The key takeaway is to pick a boring local niche, copy proven ads and offers, and resell white-labelled software, but all figures are his napkin estimates and he earns affiliate commission from GoHighLevel.

video.title: I Tried to Make $10K in 10 Days With Costco Returns

summary: Chris Koerner flies in Shannon, an experienced liquidation reseller, to teach him to buy Costco customer-return pallets via the B-Stock auction platform and resell them on Facebook Marketplace. They bid on two lots (18 pallets of appliances at about $243/unit and a 12-unit patio/shed/gazebo lot at about $222/unit landed) and then test, photograph, list and sell the items. Chris aimed for $10K profit in 10 days but took 12.5 days; exact final totals are not stated in the transcript. Key lessons: buy at a very low per-unit cost, list the best items first for momentum, respond fast, and cut prices when listings get no hits. This is hands-on physical work, not hands-off.

acquisition.how: Listing creation can be AI-assisted (ChatGPT titles and copy), but Facebook Marketplace has no sanctioned API for posting, and photos and video must be taken physically.

onboarding.how: Messenger chats can use templates, but buyers ghost and haggle, and pickup times need human coordination.

delivery.how: Physical pallets must be received, unwrapped, tested, cleaned, photographed, stored and handed over or delivered by a person.

billing.how: Cash and Venmo at handover, taken in person.

support.how: Occasional post-sale problems handled by the owner personally as goodwill; low volume but needs a human.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has equivalents (B-Stock UK, Costco UK liquidation pallets, Facebook Marketplace, eBay, Gumtree), but the Costco returns lots on B-Stock are US-centred. UK Consumer Rights Act applies to sales of used goods by traders, and sellers who resell regularly are trading, so need HMRC registration; electrical goods need PAT or safety care. Garage space and UK-sized appliances differ from the US.

He sold at farmers markets, then added tinctures, dried mushrooms, grow blocks sold to other farms, restaurant wholesale, and courses (Pro Grow Club, Farm Launch). video.title: You Don’t Need to Start a Business, Buy One of These 10 Instead

summary: Johnny Robinson (Johnny & Sergio, Home Service Academy) ranks 10 business types to buy from F to S tier using one test: would the business survive if the owner walked away tomorrow? Ecommerce/FBA, founder-brand businesses and first-timer franchises rank worst; laundromats mid; lawn care, fence/deck, pest control, waste routes and HVAC/plumbing rank higher; small ageing-owner cleaning companies rank S tier. The key takeaway is to buy sticky recurring customer lists from owners with no exit plan, using seller financing, then add systems. The video ends in a pitch for his Home Service Academy coaching, so the ranking is promotional.

video.title: The $0 Side Hustle Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Trevin, an Amazon Influencer Program creator and co-founder of the tool Viral View, about filming short product review videos with a phone and uploading them to Amazon product pages for commission. They cover approval steps (public social profile, then three human-reviewed videos for onsite placement), the Creator Connections boosted commissions (10-50%) that drive most earnings, getting free products from brands, cross-posting to YouTube with deep links, and scaling by outsourcing. Earnings claims are large (GBP-equivalent $1-3K/month typical, $25-40K top) but are second-hand or from the guest who sells a tool in this space. They started with $12.17 (a domain name and pre-order website), made $7,000 in year one, and claim about $1M revenue in 2025 with an 86% margin and roughly $3,400 of marketing spend, mostly via TikTok Shop (83% of revenue) and affiliates. summary: Johnny Robinson of Johnny & Sergio pitches a remotely run residential cleaning business: the owner books jobs from a laptop, passes them to independent-contractor cleaners who keep 40-50% of each job, and the owner keeps the margin. He claims 30-40% net margins, about $10k/month revenue at 30-35 recurring clients, and cites two students (Luis at $25k/month, a 21-year-old at $77k in a month). The video is a lead-generation pitch for a free '10K 90-day launch kit' tied to his Home Service Academy. Figures are unverified and US-centric; the key takeaway is the owner-not-cleaner, recurring-revenue, lead-gen-plus-subcontractor model.

summary: Chris Koerner argues 'follow your passion' is poor advice and presents an eight-step 'obsession audit' for finding what you are obsessed with: review YouTube, Google, Amazon and bank histories with AI; ask five friends what you never shut up about; recall childhood interests; keep a two-week energy log; map envy; write 100 questions; use a teach-it-for-free filter; and run many cheap experiments. He says passion comes from the Latin for suffering, that obsession is built by getting good at things, and that you should sell before you build and post publicly for accountability. A few small business ideas are mentioned in passing, and he promotes his Playmakers AI agency community.

video.title: The Most Hands-Off $192K/M Business Anyone Can Copy

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Lou van der Vier, a former HR worker and SEO agency owner who fires his agency clients and builds local lead-generation websites (geography plus service, e.g. towing, carpet cleaning, concrete), which he rents to local contractors for a flat monthly fee. He claims 232 sites and $192.5K in a month, with a mostly VA-run operation and 2-3 hours a week. He walks through his niche-selection process live, and describes moving to revenue share, phantom equity (profit interest) deals, and buying a catering business with an SBA loan for tax reasons. Key takeaway: owning the ranking asset and renting the leads is more passive than agency work, but it all rests on Lou's own unverified claims, and Chris is also selling a done-for-you version of the service.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; also promotes a done-for-you lead gen site service.

speakers.name: Lou van der Vier
speakers.description: Rents lead-generation websites to local businesses; ex-HR worker, ex-SEO agency owner; also does revenue-share deals and business acquisitions.

ideas.name: Rank-and-rent local lead-gen websites
ideas.one_liner: Build exact-match geography+service SEO sites in low-competition local niches, rank them in Google organic and Maps, and rent the resulting calls/leads to a local business for a flat monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Flat monthly rental of lead flow to one local contractor per site (billed by card on file); sometimes converted to revenue share.
ideas.customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (towing, tree service, pest control, carpet cleaning, concrete, landscaping design, HVAC, etc.) that already spend on ads and have a decision-maker reachable by phone.
ideas.problem: Small local businesses get inconsistent leads, have been burned by marketing agencies, and don't know how to rank in Google.
ideas.offer: Calls and quote requests routed to the business from a site ranking at the top of organic results and Maps, with call tracking, for a flat monthly fee.

pricing.model: Flat monthly fee per site, roughly based on lead volume and ticket size

price_points.label: Bigger flat-fee clients before moving to rev share
Range from weak to well-optimised sites per Lou

pricing.notes: Lou runs a few days of free leads to test a buyer, then charges a flat fee. Landscaping must generate about $8,000 jobs to be worth it. Dentists would be ideal but are hard to reach.

acquisition_channels.details: Customers for the rented leads come via Google organic and Maps rankings. Exact-match domains (geography+service.com), a thousand-plus words per page and a separate page per service, targeting keywords with 500+ searches. Small cities of 60K-400K, 'low competition'. Sites can rank without links.

quote.text: I have a thousand words on the item every time, for all services.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

acquisition_channels.details: Sets up Google Business profiles; the Woodside site was number one in Maps instantly because the name matched the keyword. Later GBPs are obtained via the contractor, which Chris calls a 'false competitor'. A GBP suspension tanked the towing site.

To find paying buyers, Lou (now a VA) phones owners already advertising on Google or Meta, offering leads for a cut. He says most reply 'yeah, cool'. Where the owner is behind a gatekeeper he sometimes walks in. Buyers are tested by secret-shopper calls.

quote.text: I'm literally just calling the person and saying, hey, I know you don't know me from Adam, but I've got customers that want this.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.delivery: Sites are built in WordPress (Weebly originally), content drafted with AI (probably Claude per Lou) by VAs and human edited. Calls are tracked in CallRail, rank reports are sent by a VA, and the leads route straight to the business owner. Lou checks a weekly rank report and call report; most sites are left alone. Buyer outreach is done by a VA.
unit_economics_claims: 232 sites; $192.5K in the last month
Over 90% net profit margin (Chris's figure), 2-3 hours/week
First six sites replaced ~$9.5K/month income
Carpet cleaning site rented at $500/month for years at about $10/month cost
Costs ~ $50K/year of VAs plus hosting, CallRail and rank tracking
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (domain plus cheap shared hosting; Lou says site cost is about $10 a month or less)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About 2-3 months for the first six sites to rank, then rent them out; the first site took about 2.5 months to rank organically.

acquisition.how: The SEO and Maps side is inbound and can be agent-driven. Finding and pitching buyers needs phone calls, vetting and secret-shopping; this needs a human or VA. In the UK, cold outreach to sole traders is restricted by PECR/TPS.

onboarding.how: Short call to agree the deal, routing set-up, a few days of free trial, and manual vetting of buyers (checking they follow up the same day, answer professionally).

delivery.how: Agents can research niches, draft pages and FAQs, and monitor rankings and calls; VAs now do these. Link building and GBP creation still need people.

billing.how: Stripe card on file with auto-pay, no invoicing.

support.how: Mostly passive; handled via monitoring of ranks and call volume plus the occasional buyer conversation or replacement.

uk_applicability.notes: Local SEO and renting leads work the same in the UK, but the examples are US cities. UK constraints: PECR/TPS on cold calling sole traders, Google's rules on fake or virtual Business Profiles, the need to disclose ranking of lead-gen brands, and smaller local markets. Buyers like Checkatrade or MyBuilder compete for the same job.

risks: Google Business Profile suspension can tank a site (happened with Woodside towing)
Niches with long contracts (elevators) or middlemen (jets) don't rent out
Finding serious buyers is hard; some prideful owners won't pay even with obvious ROI
Buyer may stop following up leads or lie about closes
Rankings can be lost to competitors or algorithm changes
Fake or duplicate Business Profiles may breach Google policy

tactics.name: Niche and city screening on Google Maps and organic
steps: Pick a trade from Thumbtack's near-me categories, favouring home improvement and high-ticket jobs
Search the trade plus a mid-sized city, skipping sponsored ads
In the Maps pack look for under 10 reviews, no website or only a social profile, and no exact-match business names
In organic results look for inner pages, directories, Yelp and thin content (e.g. ~400 words)
Compare keyword variants with Google Trends to avoid false positives
Skip the niche if competitors have dozens or hundreds of reviews

Write about 1,000 words per topic, including commercial and transactional keywords
Use ChatGPT to find common customer questions from Yelp and Reddit and add an FAQ
Add both a click-to-call button and a quote form
Use a human edit over AI-drafted copy

Started March 2024, he claims about $130K/month revenue after roughly two years. He explains why he chose cleaning (remote, AI-proof, recurring), how he grew it (reliable crews, phone sales, reviews, SEO, paid lead channels, a salesperson), and what was hard (finding crews, emotional swings). video.title: The Top Wealth Killer No One Talks About

summary: Codie Sanchez describes five personal-finance 'leaks' that drain bank accounts and businesses: payments over price, convenience spending, lifestyle creep, emotional spending, and invisible subscription spending. She gives a fix for each, including a three-number test (sticker price, total interest, opportunity cost), a 50/30/20 split of raises, an 'emotional receipt', and a recurring-charge 'friction audit'. The key takeaway is to plug the leaks and then redirect money into cash-flowing assets. No business idea is pitched.

video.title: Start This Business With No Experience

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alex Kirby, a former pastor and landscaping founder who sold his marketing agency and launched Bridgeway Global Staffing, which places vetted Latin American remote workers with US blue-collar small businesses. He claims about $100k in sales in the first 100 days from roughly 27-30 placements, charging a one-time fee of about 28% of first-year salary (roughly $4,500-5,200) plus an optional $200/month membership. The playbook covers getting first clients via texts to friends and network, sourcing and vetting talent through job boards and video applications, and a lean stack of QuickBooks plus a Lovable-built portal. Key takeaway: AI makes building easy, but distribution and proactive outreach remain the hard part.

video.title: Forget AI. Make $10K+ With These Offline Side Hustles

summary: Chris Koerner and Brandon Doyle walk through five offline side hustles framed around making $10K in a year, month, week or day: temporary construction fence rental, portable mini-mini-golf (and cornhole golf) rentals/installs, inflatable outdoor movie rentals, buying local original art abroad to resell, and flipping a pallet of auction rugs. The fullest case is Brandon's teenage son, who bought 115 auction rugs for about $1,500 and sold about 80 for over $3,000 to fund a first car. The fence story is second-hand and the others are mostly observed or hypothetical. The takeaway is that low-tech, rent-or-resell businesses have cheap entry and fast payback, but almost all need physical work.

video.title: 10 Simple Businesses You Can Start This Weekend

summary: Tim Richard lists 10 low-cost local service businesses that can be started over a weekend: dog poop scooping, fence staining, photo organizing, garage cleaning, senior companion care, graffiti removal, cardboard recycling pickup, gutter cleaning, mattress and couch cleaning, and parking lot cleaning. Most examples are second-hand anecdotes with large income claims. The main marketing tactic is a personalised flyer with the owner's face and a written price for that specific property, plus local Facebook community posts. The video also promotes the host's paid 'idea book' database.

video.title: 9 BORING Local Side Hustles Making People Rich

summary: Johnny Robinson (Johnny & Sergio) lists nine 'boring' local side hustles: parking lot sweeping, grease trap cleaning, mobile tire mounting, porta-potty rental, dumpster rental, remote house cleaning, medical waste pickup, mobile dirty soda bartending and claw machine routes. Each gets startup cost, income claims and a named real-world company example. Recurring, legally required or high-switching-cost commercial accounts are stressed. The remote cleaning segment is the host's own paid coaching programme (Home Service Academy), and the video contains a Northwest Registered Agent sponsor read. Mostly second-hand, promotional listicle with unverified figures.

lessons.lesson: Search volume combined with low keyword difficulty and few dedicated brands is a cheap way to screen product niches before investing.
When Amazon or generic retailers rank first, Google lacks a dedicated brand for the term, which signals an opening for a focused site.
Where no advertisers bid, paid ads can bridge the gap while organic ranking builds.

video.title: The Laziest AI Side Hustle Anyone Can Start Right Now

summary: Chris Koerner pitches a low-effort AI side hustle: cloning a realtor's voice with Fish Audio S2 Pro and generating pre-written voicemails in the languages of multilingual buyers, sold for about $200-500 a month. He demos the workflow (clone voice from a 17-second sample, draft scripts with an LLM, translate, generate audio, save to Google Drive) and claims it costs cents per message. He then lists adjacent ideas (audiobook narration, YouTube dubbing, local-business voiceover, other multilingual professions) and a day-by-day plan to land the first clients. Key takeaway: cheap voice-cloning tools let a solo operator sell a productised service, but the claims are hypothetical and the video promotes an affiliate-style code for Fish Audio.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; presents the idea solo and demos the tool.

ideas.name: Multilingual cloned-voice voicemails for realtors
ideas.one_liner: Clone a realtor's voice and supply a library of translated voicemail templates in the languages of their multilingual leads, on a monthly subscription.
ideas.business_model: Monthly retainer/subscription plus optional setup fee; possible free or one-off package as a foot-in-the-door.
ideas.customer: Real estate agents and brokerages in markets with many non-English-speaking buyers.
ideas.problem: Realtors cannot leave voicemails in other languages, and generic translation does not sound like them, so they lose speed-to-lead and trust with multilingual buyers.
ideas.offer: Clone the realtor's voice from a 30-60 second clip (or existing social video), then deliver a library of pre-recorded translated voicemails (new listing, price drop, showing confirmation, missed appointment, etc.) in the same voice.

pricing.model: Monthly recurring fee, optional setup fee, or one-time package as loss leader
pricing.notes: Suggests a one-time free or cheap package first to get a foot in the door, then upsell AI services.

acquisition_channels.details: Day 2: contact friends and contacts who are realtors by text or lunch, proactively clone their voice and show them the result; use their reviews as testimonials for strangers.

quote.text: Take them to lunch. Proactively clone their voice. Show them what you did at lunch so they can hear it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Visit broker offices with food and teach agents how to do it; leave a one-page flyer with QR code, pricing and URL; follow up repeatedly.
Collect five-star reviews and list on Google Business Profile after the first clients.
Proactively send pre-made sample audio files in the prospect's cloned voice before pitching (suggested as 'creepy but effective').

quote.text: Hey, I've got 40 audio files with your voice in four different languages of 10 different voicemails that you're using on a daily basis.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Operator clones the voice in Fish Audio, uses an LLM to write and translate 10 voicemail scripts, generates audio one message at a time per language, downloads and organises into Google Drive folders, and sends to the agent. About 20-40 minutes per new client.
unit_economics_claims: Fish Audio cost about $15 for 250,000 credits; the two demo clips used about 423 credits (about 3 cents or less).
5 realtors at $300/month = $1,500/month; 10 realtors = $3,000/month.
Setup fees of $500-$1,000 per new client on top.
20-40 minutes of work per new client.
ideas.startup_cost: About $15 for Fish Audio credits (stated); no other costs stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Plan suggests first 3-5 clients in weeks 2-4.

acquisition.how: Friend outreach, lunches and visiting offices are human. Cold outreach to individual realtors (often sole traders) by SMS/DM/email is restricted under UK PECR; only inbound or limited-company email is feasible by software.

onboarding.how: Agent collects a voice clip or scrapes public video; consent and voice-rights capture can be a form flow, with human checks on consent.

delivery.how: LLM script writing, translation and TTS are scriptable via API, though the demo uses the UI one message at a time and a native speaker should check translations.

billing.how: Standard subscription billing via Stripe or similar.

support.how: Revision requests, re-recordings and translation complaints can be handled by an agent with human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Technology works the same, but the demand rests on US demographics and a US-style voicemail-driven realtor workflow. UK agents mostly use email and WhatsApp, and sending voicemails or automated marketing calls to leads is regulated by PECR and UK GDPR, and voice cloning needs documented consent. A UK version would target London and other multilingual markets and possibly other languages.

risks: Voice-cloning consent and misuse concerns (voice is a personal data and likeness issue).
Voicemails sound accented; translation quality is unverified without native speakers.
Marketing voicemails and calls to leads are regulated (PECR/TCPA-type rules).
Clients may do it themselves once they learn the tool.
Dependence on one vendor (Fish Audio) pricing and terms.

video.title: He Made $60K His First Month With This Boring Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike from Iowa City, a tile installer who launched a garage-floor concrete coatings business (flake floors using polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat) around February-March 2026 with his brother and two experienced partners. He claims $60K revenue in April and $69K in May with over 50% profit, driven almost entirely by Meta ads, instant phone follow-up, upfront $8/sq ft pricing and a 10% deposit. Key takeaways: blue-collar service bars are low (answer the phone, show up, be transparent on price), AI (Claude) writes all ad copy and advises on ad budgets, and startup cost can be roughly $15-25K or under $1K by renting a grinder.

video.title: The Simplest AI Side Hustle for Beginners

summary: Chris Koerner shows a beginner AI side hustle for garage door repair owners: build an instant quote generator and a job profit tracker with Lovable (no code), plus an after-hours AI voice answering agent in GoHighLevel. He scrapes about 513 Google Maps listings with Outscraper for $111, filters to mobile numbers, cold-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, and gets roughly 40-50% replies and one 'yes' within an hour. He pitches $50 per closed lead with no upfront cost and extrapolates to $100k/month, which is hypothetical. Key takeaway: lead with a low-risk offer, validate with real outreach before building, and use no-code/AI tools to ship fast. Lovable is a channel sponsor and the cold SMS method is illegal in the UK for sole traders.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; demonstrates the build and outreach live.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering agent for garage door repair companies
ideas.one_liner: Set up a GoHighLevel AI voice agent that answers missed after-hours calls for garage door repairers, captures name and address, and charges per closed lead or a monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Per-lead fee (pitched $50 per closed lead) with possible later monthly retainer; Chris also mentions $20-$200 per lead or hundreds per month.
ideas.customer: Owners of small garage door repair businesses (Dallas-Fort Worth in the demo) who miss after-hours calls.
ideas.problem: Owners are on job sites or off duty with phones on silent, so after-hours leads go to voicemail and are lost to competitors; 78% of customers hire the first company to quote.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers calls, collects name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent callers to the owner. Free setup, no contract, pay only when a lead closes.

pricing.model: Pay per closed lead (test offer), possibly monthly retainer later
pricing.notes: Chris says he may add contracts, upfront money or a retainer later; the first offer is deliberately low-risk.

acquisition_channels.details: Scraped Google Maps with Outscraper, kept mobile numbers only, and bulk-texted 50 owners from Straight Text with a short message ('Hey, I'm here in Dallas. Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), then sent the pitch to those who replied.

quote.text: Do you answer your phone after hours? The reason I ask is because I created an AI voice agent that will
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Google Maps listings used as the lead source, not as an inbound channel.

ideas.delivery: Agent built in GoHighLevel's Voice AI with a custom prompt/knowledge base generated by ChatGPT. Each client gets a dedicated or ported phone number, a workflow forwards urgent callers to the owner (with secondary and tertiary fallbacks), and emails with transcripts go to agency and owner.
unit_economics_claims: Setup took a couple of minutes; GoHighLevel AI employee has a 30-day free trial
Total validation spend under $100 (scrape plus texting software)
Extrapolation: 200 customers x $500/month = $100k/month (hypothetical)

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and list cleaning can be scripted, but the demonstrated channel is unsolicited SMS, which is unlawful in the UK for sole traders and individuals under PECR. A legal UK version would use cold email to limited companies or inbound ads/SEO, and replies would still need a human or agent to handle.

onboarding.how: Agent creation, number provisioning and prompt generation are largely templated; a human checks the knowledge base and ports numbers.

delivery.how: Once configured, the voice agent answers calls, logs transcripts and forwards urgent calls with no human involvement; occasional prompt tuning is needed.

billing.how: Per-closed-lead billing needs the owner to report which leads closed, which is hard to automate; a flat monthly fee via Stripe would be near-unattended.

support.how: Owners will need help with call handling and disputes over lead attribution; AI can handle first-line questions.

uk_applicability.notes: Voice agents work in the UK, but the cold SMS method breaches PECR for sole traders; UK suppliers would use limited-company cold email or TPS-screened calls. Call-recording and AI disclosure rules (UK GDPR) apply. Market is smaller and Google Maps categories differ.

video.title: 7 Side Hustles For Beginners

summary: Tim Richard lists seven beginner-friendly side hustles he says he has tried or knows about: ShareTown furniture-return resale, Amazon retail arbitrage, Craigslist flipping, finding contract gigs on Indeed, Etsy print-on-demand with Printful and Canva, building a niche content following, and home services. The home services business (starting with junk removal, later outsourced to contractors) is his own and the one he favours, with claimed earnings of $3,000+ a day and seven-figure annual profit. Most other ideas are described in general terms with clips of other people's earnings. The key takeaway is that low-barrier, local, hands-on work like flyering for home services is the easiest start, though it is the least automatable.

video.title: I Told an AI Agent to Make Me Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Doyle (David AI), who used his OpenClaw AI agent ("Zach Morris", reached via iMessage) to launch three experiments over a month. A custom bedtime-story email subscription (Dreamtales) reached about $300 MRR from ~33 customers on roughly $400 of ads. An agent-built website plus postcard plus cold-call funnel for 350 Utah home-service businesses produced a claimed ~$8K MRR from about 17-20 marketing clients. A Facebook Marketplace/eBay flipping idea was dropped. The key takeaway is that agents did the build and outreach prep, while hard-to-ignore physical postcards and human closing calls drove the results.

video.title: The Best Side Hustle for Beginners (Any Age)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews two college-age resellers, Lucas and John, from rural North Carolina/Virginia, who started on eBay selling childhood Legos and thrift-store finds, then moved into bulk consumer electronics. They describe buying 500-unit lots from a European supplier, a bad batch that lost about $4-5k, and diversifying into US suppliers via about 1,000 cold calls and 12,000 emails. They claim six figures of revenue last year and say anyone can make $1,000-5,000 a month with 2-5 hours a week. Key takeaway: reselling starts with low risk (sell your own stuff, thrift, Facebook Marketplace to eBay), but sourcing is the bottleneck and supplier concentration is dangerous.

video.title: The Beginner-Friendly Claude AI Side Hustle Nobody Talks About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Dozer, a solo AI marketer who runs a six-figure SEO/content agency. Dozer explains Claude skills (markdown SOPs for AI agents) and how he packaged about 20-25 of his own into a $99 'Claude Code skill stack' sold from his own site via Stripe, claiming over $3,000 in 30-45 days. He demonstrates an SEO blog-post-writer skill that turns YouTube videos into ranking articles, a LinkedIn scraper skill using Apify, and a vibe-coded marketing OS. Key takeaway: turn the workflows and expertise you already use daily into skills and sell them as digital products, but the numbers are self-reported and the sales path leans on his existing audience.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay Meldrum, who left corporate professional services to open Swing Cave Golf, a single-bay members-only golf simulator in a Texas strip mall (Allen area). Six months in he has about 28 members on three tiers (USD 175/275/325 per month), roughly USD 7,000 monthly revenue, break-even at about 15 members after three months, and claimed 50-55% net margins. The business is run with 24/7 app-based door access, scheduling software and cameras, with about an hour a week of owner time. Upfront cost is about USD 100K, and he plans a second location and eventual scaling. Takeaway: a low-opex, membership-based, physical-space business can be near-passive once built, but it needs significant capital and a physical site.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to start and run a farmer's market (using his wife's kids' market at a shopping centre as the example), then interviews Mike McCoy of Prep Pizza, who sold DIY pizza dough kits at farmer's markets (about $60k in a first summer, part time) before scaling online via Facebook ads to claimed $3-4M of sales. The video also covers other farmer's market products (baked goods, pickles, fresh pasta) and tips such as sampling, choosing in-city markets, and filming content. Key takeaway: farmer's markets are a cheap, fast way to validate a physical food product, and a market organiser can piggyback on a venue that wants footfall.
