video.title: The Easiest Way to Actually Make Money With AI

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Corey, who sells a $1,000 'AI assessment' (audit) to small businesses. A voice agent (Annie, built on a voice-AI platform) interviews the owner for 10-20 minutes, another AI agent turns the transcript into a report (Docx to Gamma) recommending off-the-shelf tools, and a follow-up call upsells process optimisation, Zapier/Make automations, custom GPT knowledge systems, CRM setups and speed-to-lead agents at $1.5k-$5k+. Corey then lists tactics for finding customers with no following: local AI meetups, door knocking, free audits for a peer group, and office hours. Key takeaway: you only need to be one step ahead of the client, and a higher-priced audit makes the upsell easier.

ideas.name: AI assessment (audit) for small businesses

pricing.model: Fixed fee per assessment, raised over time

summary: Chris Koerner hosts serial entrepreneur Michael Girdley, who pitches about a dozen business ideas picked from a 30-idea list by Koerner's audience poll. They cover an OpenClaw AI-agent persona marketplace, paid AI replicas of famous mentors, an AI-assisted local news site, a curated X magazine, a printed YouTube book for kids, AI skincare, a 'distraction bot' app, admissions negotiation for parents, and AI audits for small businesses. Girdley's strongest recommendation is AI audits as a low-competition entry point that leads to better follow-on AI work. Most of the content is speculative brainstorming with few first-hand numbers.

video.title: The Most Passive Online Side Hustle I've Ever Seen

summary: Chris Koerner argues that simple AI-vibe-coded calculator or tool websites (paycheck, calorie, mortgage, etc.) can earn passive ad and email-lead income because they capture large search volume. He cites big examples (paycheck calculator, calorie calculator, Omni Calculator) and his own pet cremation directory calculators. He then builds an AI token cost calculator in Hostinger Horizons in about 6 minutes, picks the niche with Google Trends, adds email gating and AdSense, and publishes it. Key takeaway: build many cheap niche tool sites, validate with trends and keyword data, and monetise beyond AdSense with email capture and lead sales. The video is sponsored by Hostinger, so the ease claims are promotional.

video.title: He Can't Code but His AI Agents Make Him $5K/Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Vadim, an 18-year-old non-coder who vibe-coded Vugola, an all-in-one clipping, scheduling and captioning SaaS, using Claude Code, Supabase, Vercel and GitHub. He claims $5K revenue in 30 days at ~80% margin, with 267 paying users on $9/$39/$99 plans, acquired mainly via Twitter after Reddit/X outreach by an OpenClaw agent. He also describes running a small team of Hermes agents (CEO, marketing, growth, coding, support) and shares prompting tips, PostHog analytics, Paperclip, and mind-mapping for niche research. Key takeaway: a solo founder can build and run a niche SaaS with AI agents cheaply, but the numbers are self-reported and the product is still in beta.

video.title: This AI Finds Cheap Products You Can Sell for 5x More

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates going from a physical product idea to a sourced product in one sitting, using the AI sourcing agent Accio (transcribed 'Axio'). He validates demand for a discreet 'porch pirate' parcel box via Google Trends, searches Accio in natural language, generates a tech pack, and compares supplier prices to Amazon listings. He claims a $27 sourced box sells for $143 on Amazon, about 75-80% gross margin and 20-30% net after shipping and fees. The video is sponsored by Accio, so the takeaway is that sourcing and validation tools make starting a physical product business faster, but the numbers are an unverified back-of-envelope demo.

Ideas include an arbitrage sniper, deal feeds and alert tools for resellers, lead generation for local businesses, a 'gone wild' media account and niche 'radar' micro-SaaS. video.title: He Asked AI To Make Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Robbie, a non-technical operations employee who gave an OpenClaw AI agent ('Ron') $100 and 90 days to make money, inspired by the 2023 HustleGPT experiment. Ron's first idea (SWOT analysis gigs on Fiverr) failed for lack of visibility, but Ron scraped 200 TikTok comments from people wanting their own Ron. Robbie then launched 'AI Co-Founder Club', hosted containerised OpenClaw agents on rented Contabo servers, took $10 pre-orders and converted them to $29/month memberships. He claims about $8.4k MRR after 13 days with ~$2.6k monthly costs. Key takeaway: document the build publicly, validate with paid pre-orders, and sell to the audience your experiment attracts.

video.title: How to Make $1.6K/Day on Facebook Marketplace

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt (Jackson, Michigan), a former high school math teacher who started flipping couches, appliances and church pews on Facebook Marketplace/Craigslist, then moved to riding and zero-turn lawnmowers. He claims $20-30K profit in his first summer, quit teaching, built a helper network (drivers, a mechanic, 'Family of Flippers'), sourced volume from dealers who dislike used stock, and now runs a Toro/Bad Boy etc. equipment dealership with a best month of $1.1M. The episode is heavy on tactics: speed to lead, deposits, negotiation (make the seller name the number first), outsourcing driving first, and calling dealers for under-advertised used inventory. Key takeaway: the edge is buying underpriced at speed and selling at market value, not fixing items.

video.title: Stop Buying Things. Start Buying Assets that Pay for Themselves

summary: Chris Koerner interviews David (Fort Wayne, Indiana), a 'multipreneur' running several small rental businesses. He details a tote (moving box) rental business sold via a realtor gifting subscription, a travel-trailer (RV) rental business that made about $7,000 net in its first season, and a side-hustle recording/video studio. The takeaway is that small rental businesses need little capital, reuse the same asset repeatedly, and can be validated by asking existing operators and using marketplaces as lead-gen before moving customers to your own site.

video.title: How I Use Web Scraping to Find Products That Sell for 20x the Price

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how to use the Oxylabs web scraper API (his sponsor) to scrape Amazon best-seller lists in three categories (pet accessories, household/health, children's education books), then analyse them in Google Sheets and Claude to find products with strong sales rank but low review counts. He then finds near-identical products on Alibaba via image search and works through landed-cost and Amazon fee maths (about 30% net margin claimed on a cat feeder). He adds extra screening tactics: one-star test, fee-tier size shrinking, variations, rating distribution, Google Trends, Amazon Choice badges. Key takeaway: pick Amazon products by data (rank vs review mismatch) rather than personal interest, but the margin maths is rough and the evidence is promotional.

video.title: The Easiest $3K/Day Business Nobody Is Talking About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Sariah (27, Utah), who started Memory Magnets Co with under $1,000 in 2024 after her husband's low pay and second job left the family broke. She sells custom photo magnets online, at markets and as an on-the-spot wedding/event service, and sells magnet-making machine kits plus refill supplies and courses. She claims $1.63M online revenue in her first full year (about $600K profit), a $233K best month and a $100.5K first six-figure month after six months. Key takeaway: a simple, high-margin physical product plus a service at price-insensitive events (weddings), marketed through short-form video, grew fast, and teaching others to copy the model became a second revenue line.

summary: Chris Koerner argues now is a great time to earn from content inspired by other creators' content in any niche. He walks through building an n8n workflow on a Hostinger VPS (about $5/month) that reads YouTube channel RSS feeds on a schedule, appends the videos to a Google Sheet and emails a digest. Setup covers the Google Cloud Console APIs and OAuth consent, an RSS Read node, Google Sheets and Gmail nodes, and an Aggregate node to fix email spam. He suggests the tool could be resold, for example as a $30/month competitor-monitoring email to YouTubers, or sold as n8n templates. The video is promotional for Hostinger.

video.title: This Business Makes Vending Machines Look Dumb

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Forest, a 34-year-old former Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and beverage brand rep. He bought a failed pastry route for $15k, grew it to about $800k a year and sold it in two parts for about $185k. He then moved to Billings, Montana and started a small-distributor business selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks to independent gas stations and grocery stores. He reports about 95 accounts, roughly $50k a month in sales, 30% net margin and one lost account. The takeaway is that a hands-on, relationship-based route business that merchandises and buys back unsold stock, using local products, net-10 customer terms and net-14 to net-30 supplier terms, can start with very little capital. It is physical, driving-heavy work, not agent-run.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; owner of Texas Snacks gas station business, wholesale and retail experience

speakers.name: Forest
speakers.description: Owner of Cough Tree Wholesale (name as transcribed), a snack and jerky distributor in Billings, Montana; ex-Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and former pastry route owner

ideas.name: Independent-store jerky and candy micro-distributor (merchandising route)
ideas.one_liner: Drive a route to independent gas stations, grocery and hardware stores every 14 days, selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks by the case, merchandising the shelf and buying back unsold stock.
ideas.business_model: Wholesale resale margin: buy from manufacturers, mark up 30-45%, sell by the case to stores on net-10 terms. No service fee.
ideas.customer: Independent gas stations, small grocery stores, hardware stores, lumber yards, liquor stores and auto parts stores, mostly rural; small regional chains (e.g. 8-store and 20-store accounts).
ideas.problem: Big wholesalers drop product and leave, with no upselling or relationship, no regional or local products, and store owners carry the mental load of ordering and forecasting inventory. Out-of-stocks and outdated stock are not bought back.
ideas.offer: Visit every other week, place the order, merchandise and rotate the shelf, take over whole sections (e.g. jerky), supply products the big wholesaler does not carry (especially local brands), buy back credits on unsold or outdated items, and supply free manufacturer racks and displays. Positioned as an addition to the store's existing wholesaler.

pricing.model: Per-case wholesale with 30-45% markup over cost, net-10 customer terms

price_points.unit: per delivery at best grocery store
price_points.label: best grocery account

price_points.unit: per jerky case (some cases over $100; about $30 profit)
price_points.label: case price

pricing.notes: Markup 30-45%, so the example $1,000 order yields about $350-400 gross profit. Net margin about 30% when owner-operated, about 20% if staff run it. Sells by the case only.

acquisition_channels.details: Walks into independent stores with the product in the truck or trailer, a price sheet and a fun one-pager, and offers to fetch the display on the spot. Re-visits non-buyers every other Tuesday; the second follow-up is usually when they say yes. Early close rate about 4 in 10.

quote.text: you give them the one pager that has some fun photos. And I always tell them like, "Hey, let me go grab the product now."
quote.speaker: Forest

acquisition_channels.details: Relationship-based; owners help other local businesses. Existing accounts and regional chains bring more stores (e.g. a 30-store owner, a 25-store regional account, a four-store chain asking him to bring in a brand).

Manufacturers want distributors; one jerky brand sent a salesman to open stores for him. Called competitor owners for market insight and brand intros. Used Google to find cool local or non-saturated brands and pitched them using a list of about 50 independent stores.
Used Google Maps and satellite or street view to find stores that look independent, ignoring fuel branding like Shell or BP, and built the route list from that.

ideas.delivery: Owner drives a pickup with an enclosed trailer (now a box truck) 10-12 stops a day, about 6-8 hours, in a radius of about 2.5 hours around Billings. He is salesperson, driver, merchandiser and order-taker. Monday is warehouse day: pallets are received by staff at a local storage facility and the family helps put away stock. Invoices are made in a cheap app and printed. Buy-backs are rare because he picks products himself.
unit_economics_claims: About $50k/month revenue from about 95 accounts at roughly $500/month each
Gross margin about 35-40%, net margin about 30% owner-operated
Warehouse about $1,400/month for 1,500 sq ft; earlier two storage units about $500/month
One account lost in about 16 months
Full route could gross about $800k/yr with a $50-70k/yr driver
tools: Local storage-facility warehouse with staff receiving
ideas.startup_cost: Very low: a first manufacturer order of about $2,500 on 14-day terms (free racks), a car or trailer, and a cheap invoice app. Claimed it can be started with almost no money.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About $20,000 in sales in the first month in Billings (claimed, per host)

acquisition.how: Door-to-door walk-in sales to store owners is in-person and relationship-based. Agents could help build target lists from Maps and manage follow-up schedules, but the selling is human.

onboarding.how: Setting up a store means a physical display install and a verbal agreement, with no contracts. Account records could be digitised.

delivery.how: Driving, carrying cases, merchandising shelves, receiving pallets and buy-backs are all physical work done every visit.

billing.how: Net-10 invoices from an app could be automated with accounting software and payment reminders. Stores currently pay by cheque or cash on the next visit.

support.how: Support is an owner relationship on the next visit; order changes could be handled by messaging but the model depends on face time.

uk_applicability.notes: Independent convenience stores, farm shops, garages and pubs exist in the UK, and cash-and-carry or van-sales models are established. The UK is much denser and smaller, so competition is higher and the large-radius rural advantage is less relevant. Food labelling, hygiene registration and shelf-life rules apply. Selling to stores is B2B, so PECR is not a barrier to visits, but cold email or call to sole traders needs care. Prices would be in GBP with local British brands.

risks: Competing wholesaler can undercut and steal an account (happened once)
Perishable or dated goods cause write-offs and buy-backs
Relationships are fragile and scaling needs staff
Heavy physical driving workload, weather (-20°C) and rural distance
Brands may limit territories or terms
Chain stores are hard to enter

video.title: How to Get Your First Service Clients Paying Tens of Thousands

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jamison, a former private-equity professional who launched West Coast Decks in Southern California with no trade experience. He closed $60,000 of jobs in month one using paid lead services, and says he reached just under $1M in year one and now does $4-8M a year. The video is a tactical playbook for launching a high-ticket home service business: pick a low-decision-count, high-order-value niche, invest in branding early, respond to leads in seconds, hire a well-paid VA, cultivate referrals from adjacent trades via social media, and bid at 50% gross margin (2x COGS).

Posts daily on Instagram and Facebook plus an email newsletter; consistent branding and profiles on Google, Yelp, Houzz, BBB and Chamber of Commerce.

Instagram-driven referrals from other trades (mostly landscapers, roofers) said to produce about $400k in year one and $600k in year two; also meets lumber yards and supplier sales reps in person who send leads.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Danny, a member of his TK Owners community, who builds AI voice agents (on Go High Level) for local businesses such as barbers. He built a free missed-call voice agent and website for his own barber, which produced a referral chain and several inbound calls from barbers. Danny plans to charge $2,500-$5,000 upfront plus $200-$500 per month. His sales method is to build a Replit website mockup or a live voice agent demo before the first meeting, then reconnect a week or two later to close. The takeaway is to start with a free, high-quality build for someone in your circle and use the result as a showcase and referral source.

He claims roughly $30k of small projects in the first six weeks, then growth to an ~$800k annual run rate (about $60-80k/month). summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates building a niche CRM micro-app for independent pool service operators using only AI, with no coding. He uses Claude to pick a growing niche, then compares Claude Code, Replit and ChatGPT on the same prompt: Claude Code built it in about 2 minutes and was best, Replit took about 16 minutes, ChatGPT was fast but gave code without a preview. He then runs a back-of-envelope market sizing (79,000 US pool businesses, 1,000 customers at $20-$100/month) and outlines customer-finding methods: Facebook groups for feedback, Gummy Search for Reddit pain points, Claude deep research, Google Trends, scraping and cold outreach, and Facebook custom-audience ads. Key takeaway: niche vertical SaaS is cheap to prototype with AI, and validation and distribution are the real work.

video.title: Stop Guessing. Here’s How to Build What People Will Actually Pay For

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a 'validate before you build' workflow: he polls 100 US small business owners via PickFu on which website feature they'd pay for, then uses the Mocha vibe-coding app to build an appointment booking widget (BookFlow) in under 20 minutes. Appointment booking tied with chatbot for first place; ChatGPT analysis of the written responses suggests bundling booking, forms, price calculator and a chatbot layer, leading with scheduling in ads. Key takeaway: poll your target buyer first, mine the free-text answers with an LLM, then prototype quickly with AI and sell before fully building. Mocha is described as a 'friend of the pod' (promotional link).

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Will Cannon, who built the B2B lead-data SaaS UpLead and the e-signature SaaS Signaturely. Will describes going from a failed mortgage company to selling email lists, then an agency, then UpLead (about $1M ARR in year one, cold email plus SEO). He then explains how he cloned the e-signature category by mining G2 reviews, building a 'stupid simple' product and proving he could get customers before building. The pair also pitch a free vertical CRM monetised through payments and payroll, and both stress selling before building and that 10k a month is a life-changing target.

lessons.lesson: Cloning works best with one clear angle (simplicity) found from competitor reviews.
A strong owned distribution skill, such as SEO or cold email, is the real moat when anything can be copied.
Digital goods with one-time sourcing cost can be resold unlimited times at high margin.
A free product monetised through higher-margin ancillary services is an untapped model as software costs fall.
A target of 10K a month is life-changing and does not require massive scale.

quote.text: to build a business where you're making 10 grand a month, which is life-changing for 99% of people in the world.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Switch to recurring SaaS from agency when the recurring revenue starts to match, and keep the agency running during transition.
Building a mini brand so you are on buyers' shortlists matters for differentiation.

quote.text: And so building a brand is such a key part of how you differentiate.
quote.speaker: Will Cannon

lessons.lesson: Bootstrapped growth to scale needs good people and processes; trial and error in hiring is normal.

summary: Chris Koerner argues that a low-effort way to build a product business is to take a proven product and change its form factor (e.g. gummy vs pill, caffeine in gum). He demonstrates how to use Higgsfield (AI image/video platform, with Nano Banana Pro and Kling 2.5 Turbo) to produce realistic ad creative before building the product, so demand can be tested with Facebook/Instagram ads. He pitches several product ideas: a feminine/colourful rucking vest, nose filters repackaged for cyclists, and niche-targeted creatine gummies. Key takeaway: validate before investing by generating AI ad creative, and reverse-engineer winning Amazon products using Jungle Scout, then niche them down. The video is partly a sponsored/affiliate demo of Higgsfield.

summary: Chris Koerner tours a concrete-leveling (polyurethane foam lifting) operation in Houston with Jeff, a W-2 employee and father who started 90 days earlier and subcontracts all the physical work. Jeff claims almost $20k revenue, 30-40% gross margins and a $2,500 average job. He gets leads via Facebook ads, Nextdoor, Google, referrals, a Replit-built site with chatbots and HighLevel texting, and quotes jobs remotely from photos. Koerner shows the maths that about 36 leads a month and about 5 quoting hours a week could yield $10k/month profit. Key takeaway: a drop-servicing model, where you sell, quote and coordinate while insured subcontractors do the work, can run part-time, though the claims are early-stage and self-reported.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to sell database reactivation as a service to small businesses using GoHighLevel templates. He proposes a no-brainer, performance-based offer (10% of revenue generated from emailing/texting a client's past-customer list), walks through importing contacts, triggering a workflow, auto-replies, and A/B testing offers. He then suggests upselling other services (AI voice agents, missed-call text back, review automation, chatbots). The video is promotional for GoHighLevel via his affiliate link, and the revenue maths is hypothetical.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Spencer (Lonear Trash, Texas), a software founder who started a residential trash subscription business by pre-selling 3-month service to ~150-200 neighbours on Facebook after the incumbent hauler degraded. He bought a used under-CDL side-loader truck 100% financed, sourced used bins, and grew via referrals (free month per referral), Facebook ads (CAC $35-100), and branded bins. Claimed ~$50-60k/month revenue, ~$300k first-year revenue and ~40% margin on rough maths, with very low churn. They also discuss municipal truck auctions as a flip or list-selling side hustle, city contracts, and starting cheaper with bulk junk pickup.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hunter (Rogersville, near Springfield, Missouri), who started a parking-lot line striping and seal coating business after hearing an earlier Koerner Office episode with Sinko. In his first two months he claims about $22.9k then $46.8k in revenue (just under $50k total), roughly $20k net profit, on about $3k startup cost. Customers came mainly from a single cold email to about 300 Springfield churches (claimed 7-12% response), followed by in-person quotes. Key lessons: offer both striping and seal coating, show up in person, hire help early, and buy reliable equipment.

video.title: The Easiest Way to Build a Local Newsletter

summary: Chris Koerner builds a local newsletter live for a random US city (Roswell, New Mexico) on Beehive in about 90 minutes. He launches a Meta lead-ad campaign with an instant form, connects it to Beehive via Zapier, and gets his first subscribers within about 10 minutes at roughly $1.15 per lead. He explains monetisation through CPM sponsorships, Beehive boosts and recommendations, referrals, paid tiers and merch, with the claim that a subscriber is worth about 50 cents a month. The key takeaway is to acquire subscribers first with cheap paid ads, then sell sponsorships to local businesses. Beehive is an affiliate partner, so the content is promotional.

ideas.customer: Readers: local residents (e.g. ages 25-45) of a town of about 50k+ people. Paying customers: local businesses that sponsor the newsletter.
ideas.problem: Local residents don't know what is happening in their town. Local businesses lack a cheap, targeted way to reach residents.
ideas.offer: A free weekly (or more frequent) email with local news, events, deals and places to visit, with sponsor ads included.

pricing.model: Sponsor ads priced per CPM (per thousand opens); the subscriber side is free, with optional paid tiers.
pricing.notes: Publishing more often multiplies ad revenue because ads are sold per send, but it increases workload.

acquisition_channels.details: Meta (Facebook/Instagram) lead-gen campaign with an instant form asking for email only. Geo-targeted to Roswell, NM, with 'reach more people likely to respond' ticked, placements left open, and a 16-second talking-head phone video with captions. Started at $100/day for one day, then dropped to about $20/day. Got 8 leads in about 10 minutes at about $1.15 per lead.

Publish editions to the Beehive-hosted website so search engines and ChatGPT can index them.

acquisition.how: Paid Meta ads plus Zapier sync to Beehive run on their own once set up. Creatives and budgets need occasional human or agent tuning, and ad assets can be generated by AI.

onboarding.how: Welcome email, surveys and Zapier sync of leads into Beehive are fully automated.

delivery.how: Agents can research and draft local news from public sources and send it via Beehive. Human review is needed for accuracy, local credibility and hyperlocal facts.

video.title: Beginner's Guide to Dividend Investing: Build a Stock Portfolio That Pays You $5,000/Month

It covers stock categories (blue chip, dividend growers, high yield, growth), valuation metrics, staggering payout months, contribution milestones assuming 7% total return and 3% yield, and the 4% rule. summary: Chris Koerner and Kyler (22, Utah) replicate Kyler's Facebook Marketplace washer/dryer rental business from scratch in Dallas-Fort Worth, a market saturated after their earlier viral video. They skip name, LLC and website, post a $60/month listing, boost it for $20, buy a cheap set at a garage sale for $125, and deliver and install. In one afternoon they rent two sets for $70/month recurring in about 4 hours of work. They argue competition grows the market, a $20 boost can acquire a customer worth around $1,300, and the bottleneck is the owner's time. Revenue extrapolations are hypothetical and promotional (Koerner sells a membership).

video.title: Make $20K/Month Selling to Clients Who Don’t Flinch at Price

summary: Chris Koerner and regular guest Sam discuss one-person businesses that can reach $20K/month profit without employees. Sam describes testing an AI-written divorce book ($29 ebook, $17 bump, $300 back-end) sold via Facebook ads at roughly break-even CAC, then printing 300 physical copies until Facebook restricted the ads as 'personal hardship' targeting. Chris adds the idea of monetising the book buyers by referring them to divorce lawyers for pay-per-lead or consulting/referral fees, and extends it to niche legal books (DUI, car accident, etc.). The key takeaway is to test quickly rather than over-research, start with the simple pay-per-lead model, and that $20K/month solo is far easier than scaling to a million-dollar team business.

video.title: You Can Now Build Apps for Free With Google AI Studio (w/ Google Insider)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Logan Kilpatrick, who leads the developer product team for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API at Google DeepMind. They discuss how vibe coding in AI Studio makes it nearly free to build and ship many small AI apps, and they live-build two apps: a video analysis engine and a voice AI lead-gen agent. Ideas covered include niche single-purpose AI apps, bundles of AI tools for one persona, an AI implementation agency for small businesses, voice AI agents and a text-based AI travel companion. Key takeaway: the cost of building software is now trivial, so take many niche shots, iterate through about 10 prompts, and use vibe-coded demos as outreach. Chris states this is not sponsored but he is a Google shareholder.

video.title: Make $1K an Hour With This Simple Side Hustle

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Wesley, owner of a Grounds Guys franchise in Keller, Texas (DFW), about adding a Christmas lights installation line to a lawn business. They cover pricing by linear foot, a leasing model where the operator keeps and stores the lights, rising margins in repeat years, labour and time per job, insurance, marketing (door hangers, Facebook, yard signs) and low startup costs. Wesley claims one Grounds Guys owner does $1.25M in Christmas lights alone. Key takeaway: recurring, route-dense, leased holiday lighting can have high repeat-year margins, but it is physical, risky work that agents cannot do.

summary: Chris Koerner throws a dart at a map of Texas, lands near Flatonia/Emory, and tries to start a business there with about $20, with the rule that he can't go home until he has doubled his money. After many door-to-door rejections he mows a lawn for $20 (tipped to $30), then sells $1 water outside a fair using price anchoring to reach $38. He also spots a brokerage-style opportunity: listing a rural man's old tractor and smoker online for a cut. Key takeaway: rural markets are hard, door-to-door is tough, and the most workable ideas are simple local services, selling-on-behalf for offline people, and arbitrage-style hustles. video.title: Watch This Overlooked AI Tool Build Me a Business in 23 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates finding, validating and launching a business idea in one sitting using Replit Agent 3. He uses Google Trends and Google autocomplete to spot demand for free invoicing software for contractors, then vibe-codes an AI chat/email invoicing app with Stripe payment links and Resend email, and publishes it on a new domain (invoicefree.com). The app works after fixing email-domain verification, though emails land in spam. Key takeaway: search trends plus autocomplete are a cheap demand signal, and AI app builders can produce a working MVP in under an hour; Koerner says he does not plan to turn it into a business.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; builds the app live with Replit Agent 3

ideas.name: Invoice Freely: AI chat/email invoicing for contractors
ideas.one_liner: Free natural-language invoicing app where contractors text, email or chat a request and the customer gets an invoice with a Stripe payment link; revenue from a markup on card processing.
ideas.business_model: Free software monetised by a markup on Stripe card processing (about 0.5% on top of Stripe's 2.9%).
ideas.customer: Small businesses and contractors (tree trimmers, roofers, general contractors, home service businesses, gutter cleaners) who dislike filling in CRM/invoicing forms.
ideas.problem: Invoicing software is painful and rarely industry-specific; contractors on a job site do not want to log into a CRM and fill in name, phone, email and address.
ideas.offer: Free invoicing software where the user types or emails something like 'send an invoice for $800 to Mary Smith for tree trimming services'; the app extracts the details with OpenAI, asks for confirmation, and emails the customer an invoice with a Stripe checkout link. Includes a dashboard of invoices sent, paid and pending.

pricing.model: Free to users; platform earns a processing markup (e.g. 3.4% charged vs Stripe's ~2.9%); users can mark it up or pass it on
pricing.notes: The transcript garbles the figure ('3 12%'); read as roughly 3.4%, i.e. about half a percent on top of Stripe. Not a stated price to customers.

quote.text: I better get some sort of a lead capture, email capture, lead magnet on this because once this video goes live
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Software delivered as a web app on a custom domain, built with Replit Agent 3. Uses OpenAI API for natural language parsing, Stripe for payment links and Resend for transactional email. Text/SMS via Twilio was left out of the MVP because of US A2P registration (about 2 weeks).

summary: Chris Koerner hosts liquidation expert Shannon, who screens liquidation and government auction sites (Costco/Target liquidation auctions, GovDeals, GSA Auctions) and walks through example lots: plumbing fixtures, train sets, pool floats, furniture, patio furniture, Tesla superchargers, a Blackhawk simulator, electric buses, aircraft and lighthouses. The core playbook is to buy boring, seasonal goods, work backwards from a verified resale price, test demand on Facebook Marketplace before bidding, and scale from pallets to truckloads. Member success stories (pressure washers, patio furniture) are cited as proof. Shannon sells a mastermind and Chris sells a community, so evidence is mostly second-hand and promotional.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jazz, who runs Winnipeg Digest, a local events/community newsletter (about 35,000 email subscribers plus about 73,000 social followers) started in April 2024. Jazz explains audience growth via Facebook ads, annual exclusive sponsorships priced at about $12,000 per year, survey-based audience data, and a VA plus Claude/ChatGPT content workflow. He is now vertically integrating by selling Christmas light installation to newsletter readers, with plans for permanent lights and a fractional-CMO-for-equity model. The key takeaway is that a local newsletter is a cheap audience asset to build, sponsor sales are the hard part, and the audience can be monetised further through owned businesses.

lessons.lesson: First-mover advantage in an underserved local market lowers acquisition costs and creates a monopoly position.
Exclusivity and annual terms are the product; sell the monopoly over a local audience rather than impressions.
Own audience lets you vertically integrate and capture far more value than third-party ad networks; ad-only monetisation caps out.

lessons.lesson: Test a new vertical in a short, low-commitment window (10 weeks) so it can be dropped if it fails.
Learn the work by doing it yourself before outsourcing so you can manage labour properly.

quote.text: it's important that people get to know the weeds before they outsource
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: AI plus VAs can cut daily writing from about 8 hours to a small review step, letting the founder focus on sponsors.
Detach the founder's face from the brand if you want the business to be a sellable asset.
A time-compounding business where audience grows with the years is attractive because it is hard to lose.

quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Choose adjacent businesses that use your existing strength (marketing) and your audience's demographics (women making home decisions).

video.title: Start This Simple Side Hustle Before Everyone Else Does

summary: Chris Koerner ranks five mobile/low-footprint sauna and cold plunge businesses in the US, from Denver Mobile Sauna (5th) to Purely Nomadic Sauna (1st). He pitches the sector as fast-growing, with claimed $10-50k/month operators and around 50% margins. Common themes are Facebook ads or Marketplace for leads, partnering with gyms and studios, tiered pricing, and a free first session. The last third is an interview with Danny of Purely Nomadic Sauna in Michigan, who is only 3-4 months in and has no revenue figures yet. The numbers are mostly second-hand and unverified.

pricing.model: Tiered by duration with a weekend upsell

Website bookings; the host implies customers arrive at the site intending to book hourly.

ideas.delivery: Owner drives units to the customer, drops off, maintains the equipment and collects it afterwards.

2-3 weekend rentals = extra $1-2k/month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Rex Lindsay, owner of Cozy Pros, a Phoenix home-performance business selling attic insulation removal/re-insulation, Aeroseal duct sealing, duct cleaning and air scrubbers, mostly via Facebook ads offering a free attic inspection. Rex says he moved from ~100 in-house employees to subcontracting nearly all installation work, with a project manager on site, citing lower insurance, equipment and quality-risk burden. He gives average ticket (~$10k), margin structure (~52% gross, 15-20% net target), lead cost (~$75) and ad return claims. Key takeaway: learn lead generation and sales, subcontract the labor, and use cheap front-end offers (duct cleaning, free inspection) to upsell large tickets.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Cody Schneider about AI-powered Etsy print-on-demand: use Everbe to find best-selling Etsy products, generate similar vector graphics with the ChatGPT image API, automate the pipeline with n8n (workflow JSON written by Claude/Perplexity), push to Printify and publish to Etsy for a volume game of thousands of listings. video.title: This $15K/Person Grant Feels Like a Cheat Code

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hector, who built an online, grant-funded trade school in Texas (about $2.4M in year one) and now consults for people starting schools. The core idea is that US workforce grants (WIOA-style, called 'WA' in the transcript) pay $5k-$15k per student, so a school can white-label a course and have the government pay the tuition. Variants include embedding a school in an existing business that struggles to hire (e.g. CNAs), on-the-job-training wage subsidies, and a school plus staffing placement combo. The key takeaway is that the arbitrage is navigating grant bureaucracy and enrolling students, but it is heavily US-state-specific.

video.title: The Most Overlooked $10K/M Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews 23-year-old Kyler, who rents used washers and dryers to renters via Facebook Marketplace in Utah, claiming about $10K/month with 120+ sets, no employees and 5-10 hours a week. His 'Post, Rent, Buy' process validates demand with a listing before buying any machines. Used Whirlpool direct-drive sets are sourced free or cheap, and he also covers appliance delivery for used-appliance shops as a side income. The video ends with a plug for Kyler's paid school community and Chris's TK Owners community.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; sells TK Owners community

speakers.name: Kyler
speakers.description: 23-year-old Utah operator of a washer and dryer rental business

ideas.name: Washer and dryer rental via Facebook Marketplace
ideas.one_liner: Rent used washer/dryer sets monthly to renters at $60-85, installed free, and get paid by card subscription.
ideas.business_model: Monthly recurring rental subscription with free delivery, install and maintenance
ideas.customer: Renters in apartments and houses without a washer and dryer, who would otherwise use a laundromat
ideas.problem: Tenants lack in-unit laundry and laundromats are inconvenient and costly
ideas.offer: Month-to-month washer and dryer rental, free delivery, install and maintenance, minimum 6 months

pricing.model: Monthly subscription per set; used $60, new $85
pricing.notes: Lists at $60 on Marketplace; first payment due on install day. Customers described as not price sensitive.

acquisition_channels.details: Posts 'washer and dryer for rent' on Facebook Marketplace with real-looking photos, multiple accounts with different zip codes, and shares into local groups. The rental title breaks the pattern among 'for sale' listings. Fast replies (same day) are critical, using saved message templates. Pays $12/month for the verified badge to get support when banned.

quote.text: they're going to see washer and dryer $60. They're going to click it. they're never seen something for rent. It breaks their pattern.
quote.speaker: Kyler

acquisition_channels.details: Hangs door hangers on apartment complexes known not to provide laundry; 30 minutes per 200 doors, 3-4 leads per complex. Ordered 10,000 at about 5 cents each, expecting 1-3% response.
Word of mouth and long-lived customers; some customers keep sets for 1.5 years.

ideas.delivery: Kyler (with his younger brother) hauls sets in a small trailer behind a Toyota Highlander, installs in 30-45 minutes, tests, has the customer sign a contract and shows them how to use it. Service calls run 5-8 per month, some solved by phone. Removes sets on move-out, pressure washes, and re-rents in 2-3 days. Repairs use parts harvested from scrap machines.
unit_economics_claims: About 120 sets, roughly $10K/month
Used sets cost $0-$200, payback in 4-5 months
About 50 churned of about 170 delivered over about 24 months (about 1.5%/month)
Insurance $700/year
5-10 hours per week
ideas.startup_cost: Can be $0 using free machines. Kyler spent about $3,000 on three new sets at RC Willey and then $30,000 with wholesalers, about half his life savings or more in the first month. Used sets cost $0-$200, or about $300 with a warranty.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First install 15 Nov 2023, a day after a lead confirmed; first payment due on install day

acquisition.how: Marketplace posting and message replies could be agent-assisted but Meta limits automation and multi-account tactics risk bans; door hangers are physical.

onboarding.how: Contract signing and a demo happen in person at install; lead qualification and scheduling could be automated.

delivery.how: Hauling, installing, repairing and removing machines is physical and cannot be automated.

billing.how: Stripe subscriptions charge cards automatically each month.

support.how: Agents could triage phone troubleshooting (e.g. lint-blocked vents) but repairs need a visit.

uk_applicability.notes: Rental model could work for UK renters without machines, and Facebook Marketplace and Gumtree exist. However, UK homes typically use a front-load washing machine (often with no separate dryer or vent), top-load Whirlpool direct-drive units are rare, and landlords often supply machines. Rental and consumer law, electrical safety and insurance need checking.

risks: Facebook account bans, especially with multiple accounts
Non-binding contract; no legal protection initially
Fire risk from lint-blocked dryer vents

summary: Chris Koerner live-validates a business in about 56 minutes: an AI after-hours voice answering service for home service businesses, starting with garage door repair companies in Dallas-Fort Worth. He scrapes Google Maps leads with Outscraper, cleans them in Google Sheets, keeps mobile numbers, bulk-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, then pitches a pay-per-closed-lead offer. He builds a demo voice agent in GoHighLevel in minutes. He gets about a 40-50% response rate and one 'yes' (interested), then extrapolates to a hypothetical $1.2M/yr. Key takeaway: validate demand with outreach before building anything, though the one yes is not a closed sale and the texting method is problematic in the UK.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office, running the experiment solo on camera in Dallas-Fort Worth.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering for garage door repair companies
ideas.one_liner: Sell an AI voice agent that answers missed after-hours calls for local garage door repair businesses, charging per closed lead or a monthly retainer.
ideas.business_model: Per closed lead (test offer $50) or flat monthly retainer; possible per-lead $20-$200 or hundreds per month.
ideas.customer: Owners of small local garage door repair companies (high-ticket home service, not private-equity-consolidated) in DFW, extendable across the US.
ideas.problem: Owners do not answer the phone after hours and lose jobs worth hundreds to thousands of dollars; competitors send callers to voicemail.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers, captures name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent calls to the owner. Free setup, no contract, no upfront money, pay $50 only when a lead closes.

pricing.model: Pay-per-closed-lead in the test pitch; alternatives of per-lead fee ($20-$200) or monthly retainer, with possible contracts and upfront fees later.

Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), with a city name as a variable, then sent the pitch only to those who replied.

ideas.delivery: Build a custom voice agent in GoHighLevel (Voice AI / AI employee) with a ChatGPT-written prompt as knowledge base, a dedicated or ported local number, optional workflow to forward urgent calls to the owner then backup contacts, and an email summary after each call.

acquisition.how: Lead scraping and list cleaning are automatable, but bulk unsolicited SMS to owners (many sole traders) is not lawful in the UK without consent. UK would need cold email to limited companies, TPS-screened calls, or inbound/SEO, and replies need human or agent handling.

onboarding.how: Agent creation, number setup and a ChatGPT-generated prompt can be templated and agent-driven; a human checks business details and the call-forwarding rules.

delivery.how: Once configured, the voice agent answers calls and emails summaries unattended; occasional prompt tuning and call-quality review are needed.

billing.how: Per-lead billing needs the owner to report or confirm closed jobs; a flat retainer is easily automated via Stripe. Per-lead attribution is the manual part.

support.how: Mostly routine fixes and prompt tweaks; owner complaints about missed or misrouted calls need occasional human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: Home service owners with missed calls exist in the UK, but the texting method breaches PECR for sole traders; use cold email to limited companies, TPS-screened calls, or inbound. Call recording needs GDPR disclosure, and the UK has trade categories like locksmiths, plumbers, and garage door firms. GoHighLevel Voice AI and UK numbers work but may cost more.

video.title: How to Start Reselling (Even With $0 in the Bank)

summary: Chris Koerner hosts Shannon Jean, a liquidation/auction reseller, who screen-shares live auction listings (Target, B-Stock, GovDeals, QVC, Costco, Advance Auto Parts) and explains how to buy pallets and truckloads at ~90-99% off nominal retail and resell locally on Facebook Marketplace, eBay or wholesale. Key rules: always get a manifest, buy with math and sell with emotion, list items before buying to test demand, focus on recovering your initial investment fast, buy seasonal and boring commodity goods, and buy close to home. Several side ideas are pitched (free couch flipping, Costco/IKEA arbitrage for towns without stores, Christmas tree lot, AI manifest analysis). Shannon sells a Reseller Mastermind and Koerner sells TK Owners, so claims are second-hand or promotional and many numbers are anecdotal.

video.title: 6 Ways to Make Money With the New GPT Agent (It Blew My Mind)

summary: Chris Koerner demos OpenAI's new ChatGPT Agent mode, running six agents at once on business tasks: finding Nashville plumbers with websites, hyper-personalised cold emails to Austin dentists, competitor research for his Texas Snacks store, Google Trends ranking of business ideas, a calendar meeting-briefing task, and Amazon-review research that became a pitch deck. He pitches selling websites or SEO to businesses that already have websites, and selling AI-driven research to clients. He rates each task out of 10 and notes friction: logins, glitches when he navigated away from the tab, and slow runs. Takeaway: agents save hours of research and drafting, but need specific prompts, reference data and some supervision.

summary: Chris Koerner presents five low-capital businesses that sit around the hot tub industry rather than in hot tub manufacturing: hot tub inspection, custom spa covers, hot tub moving, hot tub rentals, and Airbnb hot tub cleaning/maintenance. Each is backed by case studies (mostly second-hand, found online or on Reddit) with revenue and pricing claims. He gives a validation playbook built on local Facebook groups, a Google Business Profile, a one-page website and cheap start-up. He closes by arguing that 'sweaty', non-AI businesses will gain demand as more people chase AI.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews a Canadian developer/YouTuber (Mike, X handle 'Rasmiki') about how non-technical people can use AI automation and vibe-coding tools. He urges viewers to build at least one automation, shares his AI pizza-ordering agent, and explains n8n webhooks for packaging automations into web apps. The key advice is to solve problems from your own industry (outside the tech bubble), use UX/design taste as a moat, pick LLMs by task (Claude for code, OpenAI for consumer chat, Gemini for cost), and keep learning tools. Business ideas are mostly illustrative and unvalidated.

video.title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

summary: A mindset-focused conversation between Chris Koerner and Shannon Gene (a reseller and content creator, speaking from Northern California) about the foundations of entrepreneurship: falling in love with problem solving, embracing fear and change, having 'delusions of grandeur' backed by action, and building a bias for action driven by curiosity and quick dopamine rewards. Koerner describes validating a private pickleball club in his metal shop with a $1.78-per-lead Facebook ad test, and Shannon Gene covers manual-before-automation lessons from Poshmark, Amazon self-publishing and obscure-parts reselling. The key takeaway is to start small, do things manually first, validate demand cheaply with math and act quickly. Few numbers are given and most are anecdotal.

video.title: If People Pay for This, Your Idea Will Work Too

summary: Chris Koerner and a co-host brainstorm business ideas built around the theme that people will pay for almost anything, and that ego stops people from doing weird, attention-getting things. Ideas include novelty competition events (horse haircut show, Excel esports, vibe-coding competitions, survival challenges), a plaque-selling service triggered by magazine features, a YouTube-to-print-magazine service, and quirky marketing stunts such as a realtor 'ghost free guarantee'. Evidence is mostly brainstorming and second-hand anecdotes, with few verified numbers. Key takeaway: memorable, talk-worthy content or events can create demand and customers in otherwise boring niches.

video.title: How to Start a Business? Don’t Wait for Permission.

summary: Chris Koerner speaks to a homeschool class of about 20 high schoolers, telling his story from selling washed golf balls at age 10 to iPhone repair stores, an LCD screen recycling business and a failed mobile home park venture. He answers Q&A on starting with no money, validating demand by selling before building (Facebook Marketplace, a tree trimming ad test), business partnerships, and his marketing-heavy, operations-light approach. The key takeaway is to sell something before doing 'procrastination' tasks like LLCs and websites, and to use constraints as a source of creativity.

video.title: AI Is Replacing Content Creators (Here’s How to Profit)

summary: Chris Koerner chats with Sam (an agency operator, Service Scalers) about AI-generated content. Topics: licensing your cloned voice on ElevenLabs for passive income, AI-generated 'boomer bait' animal videos on Facebook monetised by impressions, and Sam's stack for AI-cloned spokesperson video ads (ChatGPT, Photoshop, face swap, ElevenLabs voice-to-voice, HeyGen Avatar 4) that he says already book calls at about $10. Chris also shares a Houston billboard test for his podcast versus Facebook ads. Key takeaway: AI video is good enough to run as ad creative, and unconventional channels can be tested if you track the maths (CAC/LTV, hit rate).

video.title: You’re Not Ready for What’s Coming: Robert Scoble on AI + Future Tech

summary: Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews futurist Robert Scoble about AI, wearables (smart glasses, Vision Pro), autonomous cars (Waymo vs Tesla), Neuralink, humanoid robots and the US-China race. Scoble argues AI is still underhyped, that people resist new technology until they try it, and that this boom is far bigger than the dot-com era. Almost no concrete business ideas or numbers are given; the only practical advice is to ask AI to do market research and to find niches the big labs will not serve. The video is mostly trend commentary and speculation.

summary: Niche Pursuits host buys two mixed pallets of Amazon/Temu-style liquidation returns for about $700 (the transcript mentions $700 for a pallet) and unboxes one pallet on camera, researching each item's retail price. video.title: How to Build a Thriving Business in the Middle of Nowhere

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alan Doan of the Missouri Star Quilt Company about turning Hamilton, Missouri (pop. 1,500) into a quilting destination with 16 quilt shops, restaurants, a retreat hotel, an e-commerce site and YouTube tutorials. Growth came from free YouTube content, a newsletter, a daily-deal site and a bi-monthly magazine that repurposes tutorials. He then pitches how others could build niche 'destination towns' (sourdough, fish, cheese), and riffs on side ideas: a home-services membership, a home-maintenance subscription, unstaffed small-town bodegas, small-town micro apartment roll-ups, and a tiny-town Airbnb network. Key takeaway: build an audience and a company first, then add physical experiences in undervalued small-town real estate.

video.title: Secrets to Making BIG Profits from Small Email Lists

summary: Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews Tyler Deng, co-founder of Beehive (newsletter platform, ex-Morning Brew growth lead), about monetising small email lists and growing newsletters. Topics include niche audiences monetised through cohorts, recruiting fees and events, paid acquisition and co-registration (Boost), local newsletters, content-led brand building, a referral-program 80/20 and turning a company's customer email list into a daily ad-supported newsletter. Key takeaway: niche, high-intent audiences can out-earn larger lists, and quality content plus cheap, trackable acquisition matters more than growth hacks. Both speakers have affiliate or product interests in Beehive.

video.title: The Most Overlooked Way to Make Money On the Internet

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Freychu, a solo operator who builds SEO-driven niche directory websites. He owns six directories (three fully built) that draw roughly 70-90k organic monthly visitors and earn about $2,300-$3,000/month passively. The episode walks through finding niches via Ahrefs 'near me' keyword research (low keyword difficulty, decent volume), analysing example directories (dry ice, movie locations, towing capacity), tooling, monetisation and a cheap backlink-swap tactic. Key takeaway: directories are slow-burn SEO assets; pick low-competition niches, build ugly-but-useful mobile-friendly sites, enrich the data, and buy a few high-quality swapped backlinks.

video.title: Fastest Way to Copy Winning Digital Products (Picsart)

summary: Chris Koerner shows how to find and copy winning digital products on Etsy. The old-school method sorts printables by top reviews and looks for sellers with many reviews but few products, cross-checked on Google Trends. The faster hack changes 'star' to 'best' in the Etsy filter URL to reveal hidden best-sellers. He then uses Picsart's AI enhance and image generation to create similar designs, tests them on Facebook Marketplace or $20 Facebook ads, and moves winners to Etsy. The key takeaway is to copy what already works and change nothing at first.

video.title: This One AI Prompt Could Land You a $15K Client

summary: Chris Koerner and Sam Thompson brainstorm business ideas enabled by ChatGPT's new image generation. They argue standalone novelty products (custom coloring books, print-on-demand art) are real but short-lived, and that the bigger opportunity is selling AI-generated personalised before/after mockups to home-service businesses (landscaping, painting, tree trimming, pool, remodel) for direct-mail and sales use. The pitch is a ~$500/month mockup tool or service sold to local contractors, found via Valpak mailers, plus tracked-number revenue-share deals. Key takeaway: the best marketer and channel wins, and the B2B application is less obvious than consumer novelty products. All numbers are speculative and untested.

video.title: Build Your Next Business With This Viral AI Tool

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Max Brodeur, co-founder of Y Combinator-backed Gumloop, a drag-and-drop AI workflow automation platform described as an AI-first Zapier. Max demos internal workflows (lead enrichment on signup, support-chat digest, pre-meeting research, SEO keyword filtering, YouTube-to-blog, Meta ads competitor analysis). Chris pitches businesses built on top: Gumloop expert/freelance builder, Facebook ads reverse-engineering as a service, programmatic SEO as a service, white-labelled flows. The key takeaway is that niche workflow knowledge encoded into AI workflows can be sold as a service, but the video is partly promotional (affiliate link) and numbers are sparse.

video.title: Billy Quit his Job to Start an AI App Agency: Here's How

summary: Billy Howell, a self-taught vibe coder and former defense contractor, explains how he runs an AI app agency (Stupid Simple Apps) with a team of four, building small custom internal apps for business owners using Replit, v0, Cursor and similar tools. He describes landing his first app job on Upwork by building a demo and undercutting a no-code stack, and gives detailed Upwork tips (Looms, connects, client vetting). He advises against starting with consumer apps, shares side-project ideas (recipe generator, plant time-lapse), and discusses shiny-object syndrome and building in public for inbound. Key takeaway: sell niche B2B custom apps to paying clients first, using fast AI-built demos and relationship-based sales.

video.title: How to Make Money With Tariffs While Everyone Panics

summary: Chris Koerner discusses business opportunities arising from the April 2025 US 'Liberation Day' tariffs. He pitches a sourcing-intelligence play using ImportYeti and Jungle Scout (sourcing agent, newsletter, cold outreach to Shopify stores), offshore staffing/placement agencies, a last-mile agency finishing AI-built (vibe-coded) projects, tariff consulting, buying distressed small businesses with seller financing, and made-in-America ecommerce. He also urges not to panic and cites companies founded in downturns. Mostly speculative brainstorming, not first-hand operator proof.

video.title: How This "NICHE DIRECTORY" Website Makes $10M/Year!

summary: Niche Pursuits host Spencer Haws reviews five niche directory websites: HappyCow (vegan restaurants, estimated $10M/yr by Growjo), SoakOregon (Oregon hot springs, ~30k visits/month), Sober Nation (rehab directory, ~$250k/yr across a small network, plus an SEO agency for rehab directories), Care.com (acquired for $500M) and MCP.so (MCP server directory, 3 months old, ~52k visits/month). Revenue figures are mostly estimates from Growjo, SimilarWeb traffic and an ad RPM calculator rather than verified numbers. The key takeaway is that niche directories monetise via display ads and sponsored placements, and that a directory can lead into an adjacent service business. A Hostinger sponsor segment is included.
